docs.title: Playing Victoria 3 with scripts and excel tables
docs.text:
This project extracts Victoria 3 game definitions into human-readable tables and figures.

But visualizing game concepts is only the beginning: the true purpose is to:

  • build a mathematical model
  • translate your game objectives into mathematical language
  • solve for an optimal solution that guides your gameplay.

And you not only get to see how, but also get to see why:

  • the marginal value of each building level
  • the bottlenecks in your supply chain
  • the trade-offs between different production strategies,

all without even installing the game.

  • Build an analysis

    Set up the package, then choose a guide for parsing game data, modeling an economy, or tracing supply chains.

    Start the tutorial

  • Explore the results

    Preview every generated table and figure, download the complete files, and open the script that produced each result.

    Browse the showcase

docs.title: What the project covers
docs.text:
• Parse game data — Buildings, goods, production methods, technologies, population needs, and state-region resources become pandas DataFrames.
  • Model an economy — Translate building levels into goods flows, employment, wealth, GDP, and nominal or market prices.
  • Optimize production — Express objectives and constraints in a reusable Scenario, then solve them with SciPy's linear programming tools.
  • Trace supply chains — Visualize upstream dependencies, attribute value added, inspect bottlenecks, and compare scenario sweeps.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Released packageDevelopment checkout 
pip install "https://github.com/ShabbyGayBar/victoria3-analysis/releases/download/v0.1.0/vic3_analysis-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl"

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/ShabbyGayBar/victoria3-analysis.git
cd victoria3-analysis
uv sync

Python 3.13 is required. Parsing fresh data also requires a local Victoria 3 installation; although analyses based on the committed tables can be explored without one.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text: This document describes the layout of the victoria3-analysis repository, the purpose of each directory, and the key modules/files within them.

docs.title: Top-level Files
docs.text:
• AGENTS.md — Mandatory instructions for AI coding agents: setup, commands, external file-loading protocol, and development rules. Referenced by opencode as the entry point for agent behaviour.
  • pyproject.toml — Project metadata and tool configuration. Declares the vic3-analysis package, requires Python >=3.13, and pins runtime dependencies (numpy, pandas, pillow, pyradox-txt-parser, scipy, matplotlib) and dev dependencies (mkdocs-material, mkdocstrings[python], pytest, pytest-cov, ruff, pyright). Configures pytest test paths and coverage, and [tool.pyright] (standard mode, covering src, tests, examples, and docs/hooks.py).
  • uv.lock — Lockfile for the uv toolchain, pinning transitive dependencies.
  • .python-version — Pins the project Python version (3.13) for uv/pyenv.
  • mkdocs.yml — MkDocs Material configuration. Builds the API reference from docstrings via mkdocstrings (Google style) and wires up the usage/ and api.md nav. Watched paths include src/vic3_analysis for live reload.
  • LICENSE — GNU General Public License version 3 text for original project material licensed under GPL-3.0-or-later.
  • .gitmodules — Mounts the separately licensed artifact repository at artifacts/; the parent repository pins an exact artifact commit.
  • README.md — Project overview, features, and install instructions. Included verbatim on the docs home page via docs/index.md.
  • .gitattribute / .gitignore — Git metadata and ignore rules.

docs.title: src/vic3_analysis/ — Package Source
docs.text:
The importable vic3_analysis package. All public symbols are re-exported from __init__.py, so users can do from vic3_analysis import BuildingsParser, production_table, ... directly.

  • __init__.py — Re-exports the public API: get_vic3_directory, parse_merge (from utils), the parsers (buy_packages, BuildingsParser, BuildingGroupParser, goods, PopNeedsParser, PopTypesParser, production_method_groups, ProductionMethodParser, StateRegionsParser, technology), the analysis helpers (production_table, Economy, EconomyContext, EconomyState, MarketState, PopState), and the optimization API (Scenario, BaseOptimizer, LinearProblem, NominalOptimizer, MarketProblem, MarketOptimizer, EquilibriumProblem, and EquilibriumOptimizer).
  • utils.py — Shared helpers:
  • get_vic3_directory() auto-detects the Victoria 3/game install across common Steam library paths on Windows/Linux/macOS.
  • parse_merge(path, merge_levels=0) reads all .txt files in a directory (UTF-8-SIG), neutralises ?=/!= strings that pyradox would misread as merge directives, and merges them into a single pyradox.Tree.

docs.title: src/vic3_analysis/parse/ — Game Data Parsers
docs.text:
Each parser reads from a specific common/ (or map_data/) subdirectory of the Victoria 3 game files. Parsers either return a pandas.DataFrame directly or expose a pyradox.Tree subclass with helper methods.

  • buildings.py — BuildingsParser (Tree subclass). Loads common/buildings, resolves required_construction script values from common/script_values into numeric required_construction_points, and provides to_dataframe(), production_method_groups(), and building_groups(). to_dataframe() also joins resolved building-group attributes (from :mod:building_groups) onto each building row.
  • building_groups.py — BuildingGroupParser (Tree subclass). Loads common/building_groups. to_dataframe() flattens each group's scalar attributes; resolved_attributes() returns per-group attribute dicts with land_usage and cash_reserves_max resolved along the parent_group chain. The module-level _join_group_attrs() helper merges resolved group attributes onto building row dicts (collision-prefixed as needed).
  • goods.py — goods() function. Loads common/goods into a DataFrame with one row per tradeable good (key, cost, etc.).
  • production_methods.py — ProductionMethodParser (Tree subclass). Loads common/production_methods. employment() returns per-method total and per-profession employment from level_scaled modifiers; state_modifiers() returns per-method state modifiers flattened across the state_modifiers scaling blocks; to_dataframe() builds a flat per-configuration table combining building and production-method-group data with employment, net goods-flow and state-modifier columns.
  • production_method_groups.py — production_method_groups() function. Loads common/production_method_groups into a dict mapping each group key to its ordered list of production-method keys.
  • technology.py — technology() function. Loads common/technology/technologies into a DataFrame; parses era_N strings into integer eras and skips non-analytical keys.
  • buy_packages.py — buy_packages() function. Parses common/buy_packages/00_buy_packages.txt into a DataFrame with one row per wealth level (wealth, political_strength, one popneed_* column per good, missing values zero-filled).
  • pop_types.py — PopTypesParser (Tree subclass). Loads common/pop_types. Provides to_dataframe() and flags() (boolean attributes grouped by pop type).
  • state_regions.py — StateRegionsParser (Tree subclass). Loads map_data/state_regions. to_dataframe() flattens scalar attributes and expands resource/capped_resources into resource_*, undiscovered_amount_resource_*, and discovered_amount_resource_* columns. state_region_resource_limits() and state_region_arable_land_limit() aggregate selected rows into caps suitable for Scenario.

docs.title: src/vic3_analysis/analysis/ — Economic Analysis
docs.text:
• production.py — Production-chain modelling:
  • ProductionUnit — dict-like snapshot of one building level's goods flows, employment, and era; supports + aggregation, profit(), and profit_per_employment().
  • production_table(df_buildings, df_goods, df_pm, df_tech=None, df_pop_types=None) — enumerates every building configuration (one production method per group) and returns a DataFrame with building/group lineage, land and resource flags, production methods, construction cost, profit, employment, per-profession employment, and goods_<good> columns. Optional technology and pop-type tables add era/localization and private-wage-normalized metrics, respectively.
  • economy/ — Economy model and frozen snapshot components. __init__.py preserves the public exports. model.py defines Economy, retaining its initialization, cached properties, and public delegating methods; private helpers are called directly from their calculation modules. Calculation functions live in production.py (coefficients, throughput, and resources), consumption.py (baskets, demand, and expenses), income.py (household earnings), market.py (prices and nominal/market solves), equilibrium.py (wealth evaluation, iteration, and equilibrium solves), and reports.py (DataFrame exports, including df_goods_buy_packages() for calculated goods baskets). _utils.py shares array ownership, index-key, worker-count, and goods validation helpers. Consumption calculations share array-based wealth grouping, basket selection, demand aggregation, and expense allocation with the equilibrium evaluator; final verification still uses the public calculators. states.py defines the snapshot components, diagnostics, errors, and immutable GoodsBuyPackages objects holding aligned wealth labels and goods quantities. Basket calculations and consumption inputs use GoodsBuyPackages throughout; raw parser tables remain DataFrames. EconomyContext owns fixed production, gross import and export orders, worker counts, workforce ratio, and optional prepared baskets/scales. MarketState references that context and owns prices, deriving building finances and GDP. PopState owns wealth, demand, and optional income/expenses, deriving balance when evaluated. EconomyState composes them, preserves flat attribute reads, and derives combined reports. Economy provides nominal/market/equilibrium solving, explicit preparation, fixed-wealth evaluation, and simultaneous one-tier iteration. Immutable EquilibriumDiagnostics records numerical outcomes and financial flags; EquilibriumError retains consistent failure snapshots.
  • supply_chain/ — Single-terminal nominal supply-chain analysis. The package separates analyzer/result orchestration, cyclic bipartite NetworkX graph construction, metrics, Matplotlib/Mermaid visualization, and sequential all-goods sweeps. SupplyChainResult exposes stable goods, process, flow, workforce, constraint, bottleneck, and alternative-producer tables while retaining exact process-level coproduct attribution. Economy.producible_goods lists goods with at least one producer configuration. The supply-chain guide explains the process/configuration terminology. The design references compare graphs, optimization, accounting, and coproduct treatment with Brightway, PyPSA, Calliope, pymrio, and openLCA.

docs.title: src/vic3_analysis/optimize/ — Optimisation
docs.text:
• scenario.py — Scenario, a frozen dataclass that captures an optimisation recipe as data (goods-balance floor, fixed import/export orders, objective, banned PMs / buildings / building groups, per-building level caps, throughput multipliers, era / construction-cost / employment caps, minimum net infrastructure surplus, urban-center tie). It has no economy- or solver-dependent methods.
  • _orders.py — Shared validation and goods-aligned aggregation of fixed import and export orders for optimizers and supply-chain helpers.
  • base.py — public abstract BaseOptimizer plus immutable LinearProblem and MarketProblem compiled types. The base compiles fixed market context, throughput-adjusted matrices, shared constraints with named row slices, feasibility validation, and fixed-zero handling for the concrete optimizers.
  • nominal.py — NominalOptimizer.compile() attaches the fixed-price linear objective; solve() and solve_problem() call HiGHS through scipy.optimize.linprog. import_marginals() maps LP duals through the compiled problem's named goods-balance constraint slice, returning goods-aligned objective sensitivities to additional imports.
  • market.py — MarketOptimizer.compile() builds the nonlinear objective, Jacobian, linear feasible region, bounds, and nominal warm-start problem; solve() and solve_problem() use SLSQP for endogenous-price GDP or GDP per capita.
  • equilibrium.py — immutable EquilibriumProblem freezes household solver controls and wealth seeds; EquilibriumOptimizer uses bounded COBYLA local search over building levels for GDP, GDP per capita, or average wealth. Trial equilibrium failures are counted and skipped. Hard evaluation budgets return the best feasible, freshly verified state with explicit search status.

docs.title: examples/ — Artifact-generation Scripts
docs.text:
Standalone examples write into the separate artifacts/ checkout. Shared dataset and analysis paths are defined in examples/__init__.py; importing them does not create output directories. Initialize the pinned submodule first:

git submodule update --init --recursive

Run uv run python examples/parse.py, then uv run python examples/production_analysis.py, then the desired analysis scripts. Parsed inputs are read from artifacts/datasets/parsed/; downstream studies also read artifacts/datasets/production/production_table.csv. The buy_packages.py example reads the game installation directly and needs no previously generated tables.

Script Output collection relative to artifacts/ parse.py datasets/parsed/*.csv; datasets/parsed/buy_packages/buy_packages.csv and figures/*.svg within that buy-package collection production_analysis.py datasets/production/production_table.csv buy_packages.py analyses/buy_packages/default.csv: goods packages per 10,000 standard workers at every wealth tier, using a state with zero building levels optimize_jap.py analyses/optimization/japan/employment_sweep.csv optimize_equilibrium.py analyses/optimization/equilibrium/: best verified average-wealth solution in buildings.csv, market.csv, pop.csv, and goods_buy_packages.csv; iteration history and run metadata in summary.csv. Profitability-based restarts use a fresh --max-evaluations budget, with optional --max-iterations, --loss-reduction, and --resume controls. supply_chain_compare.py analyses/supply_chains/<configuration>/<good>/ reports, plots, and diagrams; each configuration's summary.csv; combined comparison/summary.csv with pop.svg, construction_points.svg, and gdp_per_capita.svg grouped by good and configuration supply_chain_cangshulun.py analyses/supply_chains/cangshulun_video/summary.csv, containing all goods and variants

docs.title: artifacts/ — Separate Artifact Repository
docs.text:
This path is a Git submodule pinned to an exact artifact-repository commit. Recursive clones reproduce the documented snapshot; updates to the pointer are reviewed and committed manually in the parent repository. The artifact repository and its contents are outside the main repository's GPL grant.

  • datasets/parsed/ contains parsed game datasets. Supporting visualizations stay with their dataset: the buy-package collection contains its CSV and a local figures/ directory.
  • datasets/production/ contains the reusable production-configuration table.
  • analyses/ groups study-specific tables, plots, and diagrams by subject and scenario, with shared input datasets referenced from datasets/.

There are no main-repository table or figure snapshots. The showcase, tests, and MkDocs hooks consume only the new artifact collection paths. These paths must be populated by the generation scripts before snapshot checks and the complete documentation build can pass; old artifact paths are not fallbacks. Generated collections retain their repository-relative artifacts/ prefix when published on the documentation site.

docs.title: tests/ — Test Suite
docs.text:
Run with uv run pytest (coverage enforced via pyproject.toml). Requires a local Victoria 3 installation because the parsers auto-detect the game directory.

  • __init__.py — empty package marker.
  • test_buildings.py, test_building_groups.py, test_goods.py, test_production_method.py, test_production_method_groups.py, test_technology.py, test_buy_packages.py, test_pop_types.py, test_state_regions.py — smoke tests that instantiate each parser and call its primary method.
  • test_economy.py — exercises Economy and EconomyState end-to-end (matrices, derived vectors, solve, DataFrames, GDP/wealth).
  • test_scenario.py — exercises the immutable Scenario configuration (defaults, objective validation, frozen behavior, and display names).
  • test_base.py — exercises shared optimizer compilation (context vectors, throughput-adjusted matrices, constraint families and named row slices), lifecycle bookkeeping, and pre-compilation access guards.
  • test_nominal_optimizer.py — exercises NominalOptimizer compilation and solving (solve returns a state satisfying goods-balance / building-level-cap / urbanization constraints, unbounded and infeasible scenarios raise, the retained problem/result/scenario state, cross-economy rejection, and import marginals after solve).
  • test_market_optimizer.py — exercises nonlinear market compilation, fixed-zero bounds, warm starts, objective/Jacobian behavior, solve entry points, market validation, and cross-economy rejection.
  • test_equilibrium_optimizer.py — synthetic objective, accounting, constraint, fixed-seed, failure-recovery, budget, and validation tests, plus a full vanilla production-table integration test with a small hard evaluation budget.
  • test_supply_chain.py — uses a synthetic economy to exercise analyzer validation, immutable results, cyclic realized/allowed graphs, exact flows, coproduct attribution, resource metadata, constraints, Mermaid/Matplotlib rendering, and continue-on-error all-goods sweeps.

docs.title: docs/ — MkDocs Documentation
docs.text:
Source for the MkDocs Material site (uv run mkdocs serve).

  • index.md — Purpose-built landing page with separate paths for Python users and readers browsing generated results.
  • api/ — Public API reference grouped into parsing, economy, optimization, and supply-chain pages and rendered from source docstrings by mkdocstrings.
  • guides/ — Getting started tutorial (getting-started.md) for package setup and next steps, followed by task-focused parsing, economy modeling, optimization, and supply-chain explanations. Economy modeling and optimization have separate guide pages.
  • showcase/ — Curated previews and downloads for every tracked table and figure, plus the artifact-to-example registry used by documentation tests.
  • design/ — Design notes with an index, color-coded economy calculation dependencies and storage owners, and supply-chain architectural references.
  • hooks.py — Adds artifact-checkout collections to the site and expands CSV preview directives during builds.
  • stylesheets/extra.css — Responsive gallery and table-preview styling, plus light/dark storage-owner colors for the economy dependency diagrams.
  • license.md — License page.
  • project_structure.md — This document.
  • roadmap.md — Roadmap placeholder (currently empty; see AGENTS.md for priority guidance).

docs.title: agents/ — Agent Instructions
docs.text:
• rules/python.md — Mandatory Python rules for agents: type safety (no # type: ignore, cast(), or Any), assert-based narrowing for untyped pyradox, exclusive use of uv, pyradox usage and Tree API reference, and serialisation conventions. Loaded on demand per AGENTS.md.

docs.text: • deploy-docs.yml — On push to master/main, checks out the artifact submodule recursively at the commit pinned by the parent repository, installs development dependencies, checks types and documentation coverage, and builds and publishes the documentation site.

docs.title: Supply-chain equilibrium optimization
docs.text:
optimize/supply_chain.py adds SupplyChainEquilibriumProblem and SupplyChainEquilibriumOptimizer as public exports. The optimizer validates building-level DataFrames and snapshots coefficients that map chain levels to building configurations. Compiled problems retain immutable mappings; the optimizer transforms scenario constraints and reuses the existing equilibrium search and physical solver.

examples/optimize_supply_chain_equilibrium.py directly loads the hard-coded chains from trusted era_5_automation/building_levels.csv, filters unused production units, and passes the labeled DataFrame to the optimizer. It derives target metadata from the £100,000 target and goods base prices without reading the source summary, and writes a separate analyses/optimization/supply_chain_equilibrium/ collection containing chain_matrix.csv, chains.csv, buildings.csv, market.csv, pop.csv, goods_buy_packages.csv, and summary.csv. It repeats local searches, reducing loss-making terminal producers' chain levels before each restart, until verified GDP decreases or an optional --max-iterations cap is reached. Each search receives its own trial budget; equal GDP continues iteration. Solution reports contain only the best retained state, including the re-evaluated saved baseline when resuming. The summary records each local search, a resume baseline row, and invocation totals.

docs.title: General-equilibrium economy model
docs.text:
• Implement the Economy class as a solver state for iterative equilibrium computation.
  • Implement the solver method for nominal price

docs.title: Supply chain analysis (nominal)
docs.text:
The nominal supply-chain toolkit is implemented as the analysis/supply_chain/ package and deliberately analyzes one terminal good per solve.

  • Scenario dataclass (now in optimize/scenario.py): an optimisation recipe as data (goods-balance floor and fixed import/export orders, objective, banned PMs / buildings / building groups, per-building level caps, throughput multipliers, era / construction-cost / employment caps, minimum net infrastructure surplus, urban-center tie).
  • SupplyChainAnalyzer validates positive terminal exports and an enabled balance floor, then performs exactly one nominal solve.
  • Immutable SupplyChainResult snapshots matrices, state arrays, production metadata, graphs, and solver diagnostics.
  • Cyclic bipartite NetworkX graphs provide realized and scenario-static allowed views without treating cycle cutoffs as raw resources.
  • Stable DataFrame reports cover goods, processes, flows, workforce, constraints, bottlenecks, and alternative producers.
  • Process-level coproduct attribution is exact; no implicit good-level allocation policy is applied.
  • Mermaid and Matplotlib renderers return in-memory objects and prune large allowed views deterministically.
  • sweep_supply_chains() sets minimum base-price export targets for all producible goods, retains economy order, and records failures while continuing sequentially.
  • Synthetic tests cover cycles, coproducts, alternatives, imports, resources, throughput bonuses, infeasible/unbounded cases, stable schemas, visualization objects, and sweeps without requiring a game installation.

docs.title: Pop consumption & wealth loop
docs.text: • Integrate buy_packages (per-wealth pop-need baskets), pop_needs (per-need goods baskets), and pop_types (per-profession wealth) into the economy model so demand reflects population composition and wealth levels rather than exogenous inputs.

docs.title: State-region resource constraints
docs.text: • Use StateRegionsParser total-potential resource_* columns to cap building levels for resource-limited buildings (gold, oil, iron, ...) in NominalOptimizer.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The reference is generated from type annotations and docstrings in src/vic3_analysis. All package-level exports are documented exactly once and grouped by workflow.

The data dictionary is the column reference for the tables returned by these APIs.

  • Parsing and utilities — locate game data and construct tables.
  • Economy and production — matrices, states, prices, and reports.
  • Optimization — scenario definitions and the nominal solver.
  • Supply chains — graphs, attribution, bottlenecks, and comparison.

If you are learning the package, begin with Getting started or the task-focused guides.

docs.title: Economy and production API
docs.text:
Used by the economy guide and all optimization showcases.

For returned columns, see the production dictionary and economy-report dictionary.

EconomyState(context, market, households) composes EconomyContext, MarketState, and PopState. All four are exported from vic3_analysis. Flat attribute reads are preserved; constructors and replacements use the component fields. market.context must be the exact same object as context. Components own read-only copies of their arrays; constructing a complete state does not copy its context or evaluate dependent results.

EconomyContext stores realized signed building_goods_flow quantities shaped as configurations × goods, trade, workers, and workforce ratio. It derives goods input/output totals and fixed orders. MarketState stores prices and derives building surplus/deficit and GDP from those prices and the shared context. PopState stores wealth, demand, and optional pop_income and pop_expenses. Its derived pop_balance is None unless both finances exist. Nominal/market solves leave these finances unevaluated; df_pop() reports balances as NaN.

Economy.prepare_context(context) returns a context with prepared baskets and scales, computing only missing fields and returning a fully prepared context unchanged. goods_buy_packages is an optional immutable GoodsBuyPackages object with read-only quantities (wealth × goods) and ascending integer wealth labels; it defaults to None. Construct it with GoodsBuyPackages(wealth=..., quantities=...) or clear it with goods_buy_packages=None. consumption_scales is an optional read-only configuration-by-profession array. Goods and profession axes follow the owning economy's indexes. Existing solves leave these fields unprepared.

Economy.evaluate_wealth(context, pop_wealth) returns (market, households) for one fixed wealth assignment. It automatically prepares missing context baskets and scales, calculates demand and market prices, then evaluates income and expenses at those prices. Balance is derived from the returned finances. The market references the prepared context: fully prepared inputs retain their identity; incomplete inputs produce a new context without modifying the original. Compose the results with EconomyState(market.context, market, households). See evaluating fixed wealth.

Economy.iterate(context, market, households, *, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-8) returns matching (MarketState, PopState) after one simultaneous one-tier wealth transition. Initialize through evaluate_wealth() first: iteration trusts economic consistency, requires evaluated finances and prepared consecutive tiers, and shares the supplied context. An unchanged assignment returns the same components. See iterating wealth for affordability thresholds and numerical comparisons.

Economy.solve(..., method="equilibrium", initial_wealth=None, max_iterations=1000, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-8) calculates endogenous household demand and returns a complete, verified state with equilibrium_diagnostics. Fixed goods_import and goods_export orders are added independently to supply and demand. The optional initial wealth is a full configuration/profession integer matrix. Nominal/market modes ignore these controls and leave diagnostics as None.

EquilibriumDiagnostics and EquilibriumError are exported from vic3_analysis. The immutable diagnostics distinguish stationary wealth from financial sustainability: unaffordable floor households and unfunded building losses are flags on successful results. Errors retain .state and .diagnostics for cycles, exhausted iterations, evaluation failures, and final-verification failures. Setup/initial-evaluation errors remain ValueError. See solving equilibrium for exception handling and diagnostic fields.

Economy.pop_income(state) returns a fresh writable float64 matrix of weekly cooperative income totals aligned to configurations × professions. It allocates each configuration's positive surplus using employee counts times profession wage weights, including professions with paid_private_wage=False. It adds dependent earnings from profession dependent_wage values, converted from annual to weekly amounts. See the cooperative income guide for accounting assumptions and failure behavior.

EconomyContext and Economy.solve() accept keyword-only workforce_ratio=1.0. This uniform worker share must be in (0, 1]; dependents_per_worker is cached as (1 - workforce_ratio) / workforce_ratio. pops and total_employment count workers; total_population includes dependents. Scenario.workforce_ratio passes the same assumption to optimizer-created states.

Economy.goods_buy_packages(state_or_context) returns immutable GoodsBuyPackages, reusing prepared baskets when available. Its wealth labels and quantities matrix are read-only; goods columns follow economy.goods_index order. Economy.df_goods_buy_packages(source) exports a fresh mutable DataFrame from an EconomyState, EconomyContext, or GoodsBuyPackages, copying both quantities and wealth labels. The index is named wealth and columns follow goods_index. The raw Economy.df_buy_packages input table remains separate and unchanged. Economy.pop_consumption_scales(state_or_context) returns a fresh writable float64 matrix of dimensionless household scales: pops / 10_000 * consumption_mult * (1 + 0.5 * dependents_per_worker). pop_buy_orders() and pop_expenses() accept keyword-only goods_buy_packages: GoodsBuyPackages | None = None and consumption_scales=None to reuse baskets and scales independently. Each omitted argument uses its prepared context value before falling back to calculation. Explicit and prepared baskets share the same selection and alignment checks; DataFrame basket arguments are rejected. Supplied scales are authoritative, finite, nonnegative, population-shaped, and zero for empty cells; profession multipliers are not recomputed. Refresh them when the population assumptions change.

Economy.pop_expenses(state) returns a fresh writable float64 matrix of weekly household consumption expenses aligned to configurations × professions. It prices each wealth basket at the state's market prices and applies the household scale. It does not change wealth, demand, or pop_balance. See household expenses for validation, reuse conditions, and an explicit income - expenses example.

def production_table(
    df_buildings: pd.DataFrame,
    df_goods: pd.DataFrame,
    df_pm: pd.DataFrame,
    df_tech: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
    df_pop_types: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Build the production table of all building configurations.

    For every building, enumerates every combination of production methods
    (one per production-method group) and aggregates the per-method
    employment (total and per profession) and net goods flows (positive =
    output, negative = input). When pop types are supplied, wage-normalized
    employment is the sum of each profession's employment multiplied by its
    wage weight, restricted to pop types whose ``paid_private_wage`` flag is
    true (defaulting to true when undefined). The
    ``infrastructure_usage_per_level``
    column holds the net per-level footprint: the building group's usage
    minus the ``state_infrastructure_add`` generation summed over the chosen
    production methods, so provider configurations (ports, railways, urban
    centers) carry negative values under the full-employment nominal model.
    Buildings without a construction cost are
    kept with a construction cost of ``0``.  Each row also records the
    technologies required to unlock the configuration (the building's own
    unlocking technologies followed by those of every chosen production
    method, de-duplicated in order of first appearance). When technology data
    is supplied, each row also records the earliest era at which the
    configuration becomes available (the maximum era of those technologies,
    ``0`` when none). Nominal values are evaluated at the
    goods table's base prices; the profit ratio columns follow plain division
    semantics (``x / 0`` is ``inf`` and ``0 / 0`` is ``NaN``).
    Each ``input_ratio_goods_<good>`` column is the good's physical net-input
    quantity divided by the total physical net-input quantity across all
    goods. Outputs and zero net flows contribute ``0``, and configurations
    without net inputs receive ``0`` in every input-ratio column. These ratios
    are quantity-based analytical measures; Victoria 3's prestige-goods
    throughput bonus instead uses the proportion of gross input base value.

    Args:
        df_buildings: Buildings table (``BuildingsParser.to_dataframe()`` or
            ``tables/buildings.csv``) with ``key``, ``building_group``,
            ``urbanization``, ``infrastructure_usage_per_level``,
            ``required_construction_points``, ``production_method_groups``,
            and ``unlocking_technologies`` columns. Optional
            ``economy_of_scale`` and ``is_subsistence`` columns determine
            economy-of-scale eligibility; missing columns default to false.
        df_goods: Goods table (`goods` or
            ``tables/goods.csv``) with ``key`` and ``cost`` columns.  Its row
            order fixes the ``goods_<good>`` column order of the result.
        df_pm: Production-methods table
            (``ProductionMethodParser.to_dataframe()`` or
            ``tables/production_methods.csv``) with ``building``,
            ``production_method_group``, ``production_method``,
            ``unlocking_technologies``, ``employment``,
            ``employment_<profession>``, ``state_infrastructure_add``, and
            ``goods_<good>`` columns (the state-infrastructure column is
            zero-filled with a warning when absent).
        df_tech: Optional technology table (`technology` or
            ``tables/technology.csv``) with ``key`` and ``era`` columns. When
            omitted, ``era`` and ``unlocking_tech_localization`` are not
            produced.
        df_pop_types: Optional pop-types table
            (`PopTypesParser.to_dataframe()` or ``tables/pop_types.csv``) with
            ``key`` and ``wage_weight`` columns, plus an optional
            ``paid_private_wage`` column. Missing private-wage flags default
            to true, including when the column is absent in older game data.
            When the table is omitted,
            the wage-normalized employment columns are not produced.

    Returns:
        A ``DataFrame`` with one row per building configuration.  The
        ``"production_method"`` column holds the chosen production methods
        concatenated with ``+``.  The remaining columns are ``"building"``,
        ``"building_group"``, ``"parent_group"``, ``"land_usage"``,
        ``"is_subsistence"``, ``"discoverable_resource"``,
        ``"depletable_resource"``, ``"economy_of_scale"``, ``"urbanization"``,
        ``"infrastructure_usage_per_level"`` (net of the configuration's
        ``state_infrastructure_add`` generation), optional ``"era"``,
        ``"unlocking_tech"``, ``"employment"``, optional
        ``"wage_normalized_employment"``, ``"construction_cost"``,
        ``"value_goods_inputs_nominal"``, ``"value_goods_outputs_nominal"``,
        ``"profit_nominal"``, ``"profit_margin_nominal"``,
        ``"profit_per_capita_nominal"``,
        optional ``"profit_per_wage_normalized_employment_nominal"``, and
        ``"profit_per_construction_cost_nominal"``, followed by one
        ``goods_<good>`` column per good, each immediately followed by its
        ``input_ratio_goods_<good>`` column, and one
        ``employment_<profession>`` column per profession.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a supplied technology table is missing an unlocking
            technology, or if a supplied pop-types table cannot uniquely
            provide a valid private-wage weight for each employment
            profession.
    """
    goods_cols = [f"goods_{key}" for key in df_goods["key"]]
    input_ratio_cols = [f"input_ratio_{column}" for column in goods_cols]
    goods_and_ratio_cols = [
        column
        for goods_and_ratio in zip(goods_cols, input_ratio_cols)
        for column in goods_and_ratio
    ]
    profession_cols = [col for col in df_pm.columns if col.startswith("employment_")]
    sum_cols = ["employment", *profession_cols, "state_infrastructure_add", *goods_cols]

    wage_weights: np.ndarray | None = None
    if df_pop_types is not None:
        required_pop_columns = {"key", "wage_weight"}
        missing_pop_columns = required_pop_columns - set(df_pop_types.columns)
        if missing_pop_columns:
            raise ValueError(
                "Pop-types table missing required columns: "
                f"{sorted(missing_pop_columns)}"
            )

        duplicate_pop_keys = df_pop_types.loc[
            df_pop_types["key"].duplicated(keep=False), "key"
        ]
        if not duplicate_pop_keys.empty:
            raise ValueError(
                "Duplicate pop-type keys: "
                f"{sorted(str(key) for key in duplicate_pop_keys.unique())}"
            )

        profession_keys = [
            column.removeprefix("employment_") for column in profession_cols
        ]
        pop_types_by_key = df_pop_types.set_index("key")
        missing_professions = sorted(set(profession_keys) - set(pop_types_by_key.index))
        if missing_professions:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Pop-types table missing employment professions: {missing_professions}"
            )

        profession_pop_types = pop_types_by_key.reindex(profession_keys)
        if "paid_private_wage" in profession_pop_types.columns:
            private_wage_flags = profession_pop_types["paid_private_wage"].fillna(True)
        else:
            private_wage_flags = pd.Series(True, index=profession_pop_types.index)
        invalid_private_wage_flags = ~private_wage_flags.map(
            lambda value: isinstance(value, (bool, np.bool_))
        )
        if invalid_private_wage_flags.any():
            invalid_professions = [
                profession
                for profession, invalid in zip(
                    profession_keys, invalid_private_wage_flags
                )
                if invalid
            ]
            raise ValueError(
                "Pop-types table has non-boolean paid_private_wage values for: "
                f"{invalid_professions}"
            )

        private_wage_mask = private_wage_flags.to_numpy(dtype=bool)
        numeric_wage_weights = pd.to_numeric(
            profession_pop_types["wage_weight"], errors="coerce"
        ).to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
        invalid_wage_weight_mask = private_wage_mask & (
            ~np.isfinite(numeric_wage_weights) | (numeric_wage_weights < 0)
        )
        if invalid_wage_weight_mask.any():
            invalid_professions = [
                profession
                for profession, invalid in zip(
                    profession_keys, invalid_wage_weight_mask
                )
                if invalid
            ]
            raise ValueError(
                "Pop-types table has invalid private wage weights for: "
                f"{invalid_professions}"
            )
        wage_weights = np.where(private_wage_mask, numeric_wage_weights, 0.0)

    missing_goods_cols = [col for col in goods_cols if col not in df_pm.columns]
    if missing_goods_cols:
        warnings.warn(
            f"Goods columns missing from the production-method table, "
            f"zero-filled: {sorted(missing_goods_cols)}",
            stacklevel=2,
        )
        df_pm = df_pm.reindex(
            columns=[*df_pm.columns, *missing_goods_cols], fill_value=0
        )
    if "state_infrastructure_add" not in df_pm.columns:
        warnings.warn(
            "State-infrastructure column missing from the production-method "
            "table, zero-filled: state_infrastructure_add",
            stacklevel=2,
        )
        df_pm = df_pm.reindex(
            columns=[*df_pm.columns, "state_infrastructure_add"], fill_value=0
        )
    unpriced_goods_cols = [
        col
        for col in df_pm.columns
        if col.startswith("goods_") and col not in goods_cols
    ]
    if unpriced_goods_cols:
        warnings.warn(
            f"Goods columns without a base price, ignored: "
            f"{sorted(unpriced_goods_cols)}",
            stacklevel=2,
        )

    era_by_tech: dict[str, int] = {}
    if df_tech is not None:
        era_by_tech = {
            key: int(era) for key, era in zip(df_tech["key"], df_tech["era"])
        }

    def localization_map(frame: pd.DataFrame, key: str, value: str) -> dict[str, str]:
        if key not in frame or value not in frame:
            return {}
        return {
            str(item_key): item_value
            for item_key, item_value in zip(frame[key], frame[value])
            if isinstance(item_value, str)
        }

    building_localizations = localization_map(df_buildings, "key", "key_localization")
    has_building_localization = "key_localization" in df_buildings.columns
    building_group_localizations = localization_map(
        df_buildings, "building_group", "building_group_localization"
    )
    has_building_group_localization = (
        "building_group_localization" in df_buildings.columns
    )
    pm_localizations = localization_map(
        df_pm, "production_method", "production_method_localization"
    )
    has_pm_localization = "production_method_localization" in df_pm.columns
    tech_localizations = (
        localization_map(df_tech, "key", "key_localization")
        if df_tech is not None
        else {}
    )
    has_tech_localization = (
        df_tech is not None and "key_localization" in df_tech.columns
    )

    def localize_compound(value: str, values: dict[str, str]) -> object:
        keys = [key for key in value.split("+") if key]
        if not keys:
            return pd.NA
        localized = [values.get(key) for key in keys]
        if any(item is None for item in localized):
            return pd.NA
        return "+".join(item for item in localized if item is not None)

    pm_keys = df_pm["production_method"].tolist()
    pm_techs = [_tech_keys(value) for value in df_pm["unlocking_technologies"]]
    pm_eras = (
        [_era_of_techs(techs, era_by_tech) for techs in pm_techs]
        if df_tech is not None
        else []
    )

    group_positions: dict[tuple[str, str], list[int]] = {}
    for position, (building, group) in enumerate(
        zip(df_pm["building"], df_pm["production_method_group"])
    ):
        group_positions.setdefault((building, group), []).append(position)

    building_columns = [
        "key",
        "building_group",
        "urbanization",
        "infrastructure_usage_per_level",
        "required_construction_points",
        "production_method_groups",
        "unlocking_technologies",
    ]
    economy_of_scale = (
        df_buildings["economy_of_scale"].fillna(False).eq(True)
        if "economy_of_scale" in df_buildings.columns
        else pd.Series(False, index=df_buildings.index)
    )
    is_subsistence = (
        df_buildings["is_subsistence"].fillna(False).eq(True)
        if "is_subsistence" in df_buildings.columns
        else pd.Series(False, index=df_buildings.index)
    )
    economy_of_scale_eligible = economy_of_scale & ~is_subsistence
    combo_rows: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    membership: list[tuple[int, int]] = []

    for (
        building,
        building_group,
        urbanization,
        infrastructure,
        construction_cost,
        pmg_value,
        unlock_value,
        has_economy_of_scale,
    ) in zip(
        *[df_buildings[column] for column in building_columns],
        economy_of_scale_eligible,
    ):
        if not isinstance(pmg_value, str) or not pmg_value:
            warnings.warn(
                f"Building {building} has no production method groups, skipped",
                stacklevel=2,
            )
            continue

        groups: list[list[int]] = []
        for pmg in pmg_value.split("+"):
            positions = group_positions.get((building, pmg))
            if not positions:
                warnings.warn(
                    f"Building {building} has no production methods in group "
                    f"{pmg}, skipped",
                    stacklevel=2,
                )
                groups = []
                break
            groups.append(positions)
        if not groups:
            continue

        building_techs = _tech_keys(unlock_value)
        building_era = (
            _era_of_techs(building_techs, era_by_tech) if df_tech is not None else 0
        )
        if pd.isna(construction_cost):
            construction_cost = 0
        if pd.isna(urbanization):
            urbanization = 0.0
        if pd.isna(infrastructure):
            infrastructure = 0.0

        for positions in product(*groups):
            combo_id = len(combo_rows)
            era = building_era
            techs = list(building_techs)
            for position in positions:
                if df_tech is not None:
                    era = max(era, pm_eras[position])
                techs.extend(pm_techs[position])
            combo_rows.append(
                {
                    "building": building,
                    "production_method": "+".join(
                        pm_keys[position] for position in positions
                    ),
                    "building_group": building_group,
                    "economy_of_scale": bool(has_economy_of_scale),
                    "urbanization": urbanization,
                    "infrastructure_usage_per_level": infrastructure,
                    "unlocking_tech": "+".join(dict.fromkeys(techs)),
                    "construction_cost": int(construction_cost),
                }
            )
            if df_tech is not None:
                combo_rows[-1]["era"] = era
            if has_building_localization:
                combo_rows[-1]["building_localization"] = building_localizations.get(
                    str(building), pd.NA
                )
            if has_pm_localization:
                pm_value = "+".join(pm_keys[position] for position in positions)
                combo_rows[-1]["production_method_localization"] = localize_compound(
                    pm_value, pm_localizations
                )
            if has_building_group_localization:
                combo_rows[-1]["building_group_localization"] = (
                    building_group_localizations.get(str(building_group), pd.NA)
                )
            if has_tech_localization:
                combo_rows[-1]["unlocking_tech_localization"] = localize_compound(
                    "+".join(dict.fromkeys(techs)), tech_localizations
                )
            membership.extend((combo_id, position) for position in positions)

    building_metadata_defaults = {
        "parent_group": pd.NA,
        "land_usage": pd.NA,
        "is_subsistence": False,
        "discoverable_resource": False,
        "depletable_resource": False,
    }
    column_order = [
        "building",
        *(["building_localization"] if has_building_localization else []),
        "production_method",
        *(["production_method_localization"] if has_pm_localization else []),
        "building_group",
        *(["building_group_localization"] if has_building_group_localization else []),
        *building_metadata_defaults,
        "economy_of_scale",
        "urbanization",
        "infrastructure_usage_per_level",
        *(["era"] if df_tech is not None else []),
        "unlocking_tech",
        *(["unlocking_tech_localization"] if has_tech_localization else []),
        "employment",
        *(["wage_normalized_employment"] if wage_weights is not None else []),
        "construction_cost",
        "value_goods_inputs_nominal",
        "value_goods_outputs_nominal",
        "profit_nominal",
        "profit_margin_nominal",
        "profit_per_capita_nominal",
        *(
            ["profit_per_wage_normalized_employment_nominal"]
            if wage_weights is not None
            else []
        ),
        "profit_per_construction_cost_nominal",
        *goods_and_ratio_cols,
        *profession_cols,
    ]
    if not combo_rows:
        empty = pd.DataFrame(columns=column_order)
        for column in column_order:
            if column.endswith("_localization"):
                empty[column] = empty[column].astype("string")
            elif column in input_ratio_cols:
                empty[column] = empty[column].astype(np.float64)
        return empty

    member_positions = [position for _, position in membership]
    combo_ids = [combo_id for combo_id, _ in membership]
    members = df_pm.iloc[member_positions]
    sums = (
        members.groupby(np.asarray(combo_ids), sort=True)[sum_cols]
        .sum()
        .reset_index(drop=True)
    )

    result = pd.concat([pd.DataFrame(combo_rows), sums], axis=1)

    for column, default in building_metadata_defaults.items():
        if column in df_buildings.columns:
            values: dict[str, object] = {
                str(key): value
                for key, value in zip(df_buildings["key"], df_buildings[column])
            }
            result[column] = result["building"].map(
                lambda building, values=values, default=default: values.get(
                    str(building), default
                )
            )
            if isinstance(default, bool):
                result[column] = result[column].fillna(default).eq(True)
        else:
            result[column] = default

    result["infrastructure_usage_per_level"] = (
        result["infrastructure_usage_per_level"] - result["state_infrastructure_add"]
    )
    if wage_weights is not None:
        result["wage_normalized_employment"] = (
            result[profession_cols].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64) @ wage_weights
        )

    prices = df_goods["cost"].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
    flows = result[goods_cols].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
    input_quantities = np.maximum(-flows, 0.0)
    input_quantity_totals = input_quantities.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    input_ratios = np.divide(
        input_quantities,
        input_quantity_totals,
        out=np.zeros_like(input_quantities),
        where=input_quantity_totals != 0,
    )
    result = pd.concat(
        [
            result,
            pd.DataFrame(
                input_ratios,
                columns=input_ratio_cols,
                index=result.index,
            ),
        ],
        axis=1,
    )
    result["value_goods_inputs_nominal"] = input_quantities @ prices
    result["value_goods_outputs_nominal"] = np.maximum(flows, 0.0) @ prices
    result["profit_nominal"] = (
        result["value_goods_outputs_nominal"] - result["value_goods_inputs_nominal"]
    )
    result["profit_margin_nominal"] = (
        result["profit_nominal"] / result["value_goods_outputs_nominal"]
    )
    result["profit_per_capita_nominal"] = (
        result["profit_nominal"] / result["employment"]
    )
    if wage_weights is not None:
        result["profit_per_wage_normalized_employment_nominal"] = (
            result["profit_nominal"] / result["wage_normalized_employment"]
        )
    result["profit_per_construction_cost_nominal"] = (
        result["profit_nominal"] / result["construction_cost"]
    )

    result = result.reindex(columns=column_order)
    for column in column_order:
        if column.endswith("_localization"):
            result[column] = result[column].astype("string")
    return result

Builds EconomyState instances from building-level vectors.

Wraps production, goods, pop-types, pop-needs, and buy-package tables parsed from the Victoria 3 game files and lazily caches the coefficients needed to derive prices, supply, demand, employment, and wealth for a given building_levels vector.

Input tables are defensively copied. Public DataFrames remain mutable, but editing them is unsupported because cached coefficients are not invalidated. Construct a new Economy when model data changes. Cached indexes are tuples and cached arrays are owned and read-only. Starting wealth uses int64; other numeric coefficients use float64.

def __init__(
    self,
    game_dir: str | Path | None = None,
    df_production: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
    df_goods: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
    df_pop_types: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
    *,
    df_pop_needs: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
    df_buy_packages: pd.DataFrame | None = None,
    language: str | None = None,
):
    """Initialise the model by parsing the required game tables.

    Args:
        game_dir: Path to the Victoria 3 ``game`` directory. If ``None``
            the directory is located automatically via
            `get_vic3_directory`. Ignored for
            any table whose DataFrame is passed directly.
        df_production: Pre-built production table DataFrame. When
            provided, overrides the table that would otherwise be generated
            by `production_table`. Useful for reusing a
            filtered or cached table.
        df_goods: Pre-built goods table DataFrame. When provided,
            overrides the table that would otherwise be generated by
            `goods`.
        df_pop_types: Pre-built pop-types table DataFrame. When provided,
            overrides the table that would otherwise be generated by
            `PopTypesParser`.
        df_pop_needs: Pre-built substitution definitions. When omitted,
            parsed by `PopNeedsParser`.
        df_buy_packages: Pre-built wealth packages. When omitted, parsed
            by `buy_packages`.
        language: Optional Victoria 3 localization language used only when
            parsing tables internally. Explicit DataFrames are authoritative
            and are not modified.
    """
    if df_goods is None:
        df_goods = goods(game_dir, language=language)
    if df_pop_types is None:
        df_pop_types = PopTypesParser(game_dir).to_dataframe(language=language)
    if df_pop_needs is None:
        df_pop_needs = PopNeedsParser(game_dir).to_dataframe(language=language)
    if df_buy_packages is None:
        df_buy_packages = buy_packages(game_dir)
    if df_production is None:
        df_production = production_table(
            BuildingsParser(game_dir).to_dataframe(language=language),
            df_goods,
            ProductionMethodParser(game_dir).to_dataframe(language=language),
            technology(game_dir, language=language),
            df_pop_types,
        )
    object.__setattr__(self, "df_production", df_production.copy(deep=True))
    object.__setattr__(self, "df_goods", df_goods.copy(deep=True))
    object.__setattr__(self, "df_pop_types", df_pop_types.copy(deep=True))
    object.__setattr__(self, "df_pop_needs", df_pop_needs.copy(deep=True))
    object.__setattr__(self, "df_buy_packages", df_buy_packages.copy(deep=True))
    _production._fill_production_metadata_defaults(self)
    goods_columns = [f"goods_{good}" for good in self.goods_index]

    missing = set(goods_columns) - set(self.df_production.columns)
    if missing:
        warnings.warn(f"Missing goods input columns: {sorted(missing)}")

def economy_of_scale_bonuses(
    self,
    building_levels: np.ndarray[tuple[int], np.dtype[np.float64]],
    level_cap: float = 20.0,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return per-configuration economy-of-scale throughput bonuses.

    Levels are summed across all production-method configurations of each
    building. Eligible configurations receive one percentage point of
    throughput per total building level, capped by *level_cap*. Returned
    values are additive bonuses (for example, ``0.2`` for +20%), not full
    multipliers.

    Args:
        building_levels: Production-row-aligned building levels.
        level_cap: Maximum number of levels contributing to the bonus.

    Returns:
        A 1-D bonus vector aligned to the production table.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If *building_levels* is not aligned to the production
            table or *level_cap* is negative or non-finite.
    """
    return _production.economy_of_scale_bonuses(self, building_levels, level_cap)

def evaluate_wealth(
    self, context: EconomyContext, pop_wealth: np.ndarray
) -> tuple[MarketState, PopState]:
    """Evaluate demand, market prices, and finances at fixed household wealth.

    Prepare missing context baskets and consumption scales, preserving any
    supplied prepared fields. Calculate demand first, then market prices
    from total buy orders and fixed sell orders, and finally cooperative
    income and household expenses at those same prices.

    Args:
        context: Fixed production, trade, and worker counts aligned to this
            economy. Prepared baskets and scales are optional.
        pop_wealth: Non-negative integer wealth matrix aligned to
            configurations and professions. Occupied tiers need baskets;
            empty cells may use undefined tiers.

    Returns:
        Matching market and household components, in that order, with
        read-only arrays and fully evaluated household finances. Wealth
        values are preserved. The market shares the supplied context when
        fully prepared; otherwise it references a newly prepared context.
        Compose a complete snapshot with
        ``EconomyState(market.context, market, households)``.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If context inputs or wealth are invalid or misaligned,
            preparation fails, occupied tiers lack baskets, income cannot
            be allocated, or calculated results are non-finite.

    Notes:
        Inputs and model tables are unchanged. This evaluates one wealth
        assignment without affordability limits or wealth transitions.
    """
    return _equilibrium.evaluate_wealth(self, context, pop_wealth)

def iterate(
    self,
    context: EconomyContext,
    market: MarketState,
    households: PopState,
    *,
    rtol: float = 1e-9,
    atol: float = 1e-8,
) -> tuple[MarketState, PopState]:
    """Apply one simultaneous wealth transition and evaluate matching results.

    Initialize with ``evaluate_wealth()`` and pass its prepared market context.
    Inputs must be consistent: this method validates alignment and finances,
    but trusts their economic consistency without reevaluating the old wealth.
    Decrease below 98% of current cost; otherwise increase at or above 102%
    of next-tier cost, using previous prices and household scales. Each
    threshold accepts equality within ``atol + rtol * max(income, threshold)``.
    Decreases take precedence. Empty cells and bounded tiers are preserved.

    Returns:
        Matching read-only market and population components sharing ``context``.
        If wealth is unchanged, the exact supplied components are returned.
        A step is numerical rather than a simulated week and makes no
        convergence or financial-sustainability claim.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If tolerances, context identity, prepared tiers, component
            axes, prices, or finances are invalid, or calculations fail.
    """
    return _equilibrium.iterate(
        self, context, market, households, rtol=rtol, atol=atol
    )

def goods_buy_packages(
    self, state: EconomyState | EconomyContext
) -> GoodsBuyPackages:
    """Calculate weekly goods packages per 10,000 standard workers by wealth.

    Convert the model's wealth-by-category values to goods quantities using
    the supplied state's substitution shares and the model's base prices:
    ``wealth_category_values @ category_purchase_shares / base_prices``.
    Substitution uses effective supply, configured weights, minimum/maximum
    supply shares, and default goods as described by `pop_buy_orders`.

    Args:
        state: Snapshot or context aligned to this economy. Prepared
            context baskets are reused when present; otherwise only
            building inputs/outputs, imports, and exports are used.

    Returns:
        Immutable `GoodsBuyPackages` with ascending int64 ``wealth`` labels and
        read-only float64 ``quantities`` in `goods_index` column order.
        Prepared context baskets are returned unchanged after validating
        goods alignment; otherwise all tiers in ``df_buy_packages`` are
        calculated. Quantities are goods units per week per 10,000 standard
        workers, with zero for unconsumed goods. Inputs are unchanged.
        Use `Economy.df_goods_buy_packages` for a mutable DataFrame export.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If goods flows are misaligned, negative, or non-finite,
            base prices are not positive, or package/substitution
            definitions are invalid or reference missing categories/goods.

    Notes:
        Packages are independent of represented population, workforce ratio,
        occupied wealth, profession consumption multipliers, market prices,
        and existing population demand. Culture, prestige goods, local-state
        effects, and weekly adjustment are not modeled.
        Subtracting half of non-pop demand from supply is community-derived,
        documented by the Needs wiki rather than game-file comments.
        Clamping negative effective supply to zero is a model convention.

    References:
        - ``common/buy_packages/00_buy_packages.txt``: category values by
          integer wealth.
        - ``common/pop_needs/00_pop_needs.txt``: substitution weights,
          supply-share limits, and default goods.
        - [Needs wiki, Formulas](https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/Needs#Formulas):
          scaling per 10,000 workers and substitution, including the
          community-derived half-non-pop-demand deduction.
        - [Official developer diary #13](https://steamcommunity.com/games/529340/announcements/detail/2965045886379003737):
          wealth-dependent needs and valuation at goods' base prices.
    """
    return _consumption.goods_buy_packages(self, state)

def pop_consumption_scales(
    self, state: EconomyState | EconomyContext
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return household consumption as multiples of a standard buy package.

    Calculate ``pops / 10_000 * consumption_mult * (1 + 0.5 *
    dependents_per_worker)``. Missing profession multipliers default to one.
    Workers and dependents share a wealth tier; dependents consume half as
    much per person. Wealth values, prices, and goods flows are not used.

    Args:
        state: Snapshot or context with aligned worker counts. Prepared
            context scales are copied when present. Snapshot wealth must
            also have the population shape.

    Returns:
        A fresh, owned, writable float64 matrix aligned to configurations
        and professions. Values are dimensionless multiples of weekly
        goods packages per 10,000 standard workers. Reuse them while worker
        counts, workforce ratio, and profession multipliers remain fixed.
        The state and model tables are unchanged.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If household shapes, worker counts, profession keys,
            or consumption multipliers are invalid, or scales overflow.

pop_buy_orders(
    state: EconomyState,
    *,
    goods_buy_packages: GoodsBuyPackages | None = None,
    consumption_scales: ndarray | None = None,
) -> ndarray

Calculate weekly population buy orders for the represented workers.

Prepared context baskets and scales are reused when their explicit arguments are omitted. Without prepared baskets, each need category's effective supply is max(sell_orders - 0.5 * (building_goods_input + exports), 0). Divide each eligible good's effective supply by the category total, clip that share to its configured minimum and maximum, multiply by its configured weight, and normalize these purchase weights. Share limits apply before normalization; they do not cap final purchases. With zero effective supply, start from zero shares, retaining any configured minimum shares. If all purchase weights are zero, use the category's default good exclusively.

Each occupied cell's integer wealth selects a buy package, whose category values are measured in pounds at base prices per 10,000 workers. Multiply worker counts by 1 + 0.5 * dependents_per_worker, scale by consumption_mult / 10_000, distribute by normalized purchase weights, and divide by goods' base prices to obtain units per week. Household scales are aggregated by wealth before allocating goods baskets, without a building-by-profession-by-goods tensor.

Parameters:

Returns:

  • ndarray –

    A fresh writable float64 vector of shape (n_goods,) aligned

  • ndarray –

    to goods_index, suitable for PopState.pop_buy_orders.

  • ndarray –

    The state is unchanged.

Raises:

  • TypeError –

    If supplied baskets are not a GoodsBuyPackages instance.

  • ValueError –

    If relevant state arrays are misaligned, quantities are negative or non-finite, base prices are not positive, occupied wealth tiers are undefined, or model tables have invalid definitions or missing category/goods references. Also raised for invalid supplied package labels, quantities, or consumption scales, or non-finite calculated demand.

Notes

The half-non-pop-demand deduction is community-derived and documented by the Needs wiki; it is not confirmed by the comments in the game files. Clamping negative effective supply to zero is this model's convention. This is target consumption, without weekly adjustment, culture, prestige goods, local-state effects, demographic changes, or wealth feedback. Market prices and existing state.pop_buy_orders do not influence the result.

References
  • common/pop_needs/00_pop_needs.txt: substitution weights, minimum/maximum supply shares, comments on their meaning, and default goods.
  • common/buy_packages/00_buy_packages.txt: category values indexed by integer wealth.
  • common/pop_types/: profession consumption_mult values.
  • Needs wiki, Formulas: population scaling and detailed substitution formulas. The non-pop-demand deduction is attributed there to community reverse engineering: https://www.reddit.com/r/victoria3/comments/yudc80/pop_needs_consumer_good_substitution_and_why_oil/
  • Official developer diary #13: wealth-dependent needs and valuation using goods' base prices.

    self,
    state: EconomyState,
    *,
    goods_buy_packages: GoodsBuyPackages | None = None,
    consumption_scales: np.ndarray | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Calculate weekly population buy orders for the represented workers.

    Prepared context baskets and scales are reused when their explicit
    arguments are omitted. Without prepared baskets, each need category's
    effective supply is
    ``max(sell_orders - 0.5 * (building_goods_input + exports), 0)``.
    Divide each eligible good's effective supply by the category total,
    clip that share to its configured minimum and maximum, multiply by
    its configured weight, and normalize these purchase weights. Share
    limits apply before normalization; they do not cap final purchases.
    With zero effective supply, start from zero shares, retaining any
    configured minimum shares. If all purchase weights are zero, use the
    category's default good exclusively.

    Each occupied cell's integer wealth selects a buy package, whose
    category values are measured in pounds at base prices per 10,000
    workers. Multiply worker counts by ``1 + 0.5 * dependents_per_worker``,
    scale by ``consumption_mult / 10_000``, distribute by
    normalized purchase weights, and divide by goods' base prices to
    obtain units per week. Household scales are aggregated by wealth before
    allocating goods baskets, without a building-by-profession-by-goods tensor.

    Args:
        state: Snapshot aligned to this economy's building, profession,
            and goods indexes. Workers and their dependents consume at the
            same wealth tier; dependents consume half as much per person.
            Empty cells need no wealth package.
        goods_buy_packages: Optional immutable `GoodsBuyPackages`, as returned by
            `goods_buy_packages`. Wealth labels must cover every occupied
            tier. Quantity columns must follow `goods_index` order; column
            count is checked against the economy. Construction validates and
            sorts wealth labels and quantities together. Supplied baskets
            are scaled directly by worker-
            equivalent population and profession consumption multipliers,
            without substitution or base-price conversion, and remain fixed
            when supply changes.
            Unused state goods flows and raw need/package tables are not
            validated in this mode. The baskets are unchanged.
        consumption_scales: Optional precomputed matrix returned by
            `pop_consumption_scales`. Supplied values are
            authoritative, finite, non-negative, and shaped like ``pops``;
            empty cells must have zero scale. They already include all
            population factors, so profession multipliers are not read or
            reapplied. The caller ensures scales remain valid for the
            population assumptions. The matrix is unchanged.

    Returns:
        A fresh writable float64 vector of shape ``(n_goods,)`` aligned
        to `goods_index`, suitable for ``PopState.pop_buy_orders``.
        The state is unchanged.

    Raises:
        TypeError: If supplied baskets are not a `GoodsBuyPackages` instance.
        ValueError: If relevant state arrays are misaligned, quantities
            are negative or non-finite, base prices are not positive,
            occupied wealth tiers are undefined, or model tables have
            invalid definitions or missing category/goods references. Also
            raised for invalid supplied package labels, quantities, or
            consumption scales, or non-finite calculated demand.

    Notes:
        The half-non-pop-demand deduction is community-derived and
        documented by the Needs wiki; it is not confirmed by the comments
        in the game files. Clamping negative effective supply to zero is
        this model's convention. This is target consumption, without
        weekly adjustment, culture, prestige goods, local-state effects,
        demographic changes, or wealth feedback. Market prices and
        existing ``state.pop_buy_orders`` do not influence the result.

    References:
        - ``common/pop_needs/00_pop_needs.txt``: substitution weights,
          minimum/maximum supply shares, comments on their meaning, and
          default goods.
        - ``common/buy_packages/00_buy_packages.txt``: category values
          indexed by integer wealth.
        - ``common/pop_types/``: profession ``consumption_mult`` values.
        - [Needs wiki, Formulas](https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/Needs#Formulas):
          population scaling and detailed substitution formulas. The
          non-pop-demand deduction is attributed there to community
          reverse engineering:
          https://www.reddit.com/r/victoria3/comments/yudc80/pop_needs_consumer_good_substitution_and_why_oil/
        - [Official developer diary #13](https://steamcommunity.com/games/529340/announcements/detail/2965045886379003737):
          wealth-dependent needs and valuation using goods' base prices.
    """
    return _consumption.pop_buy_orders(
        self,
        state,
        goods_buy_packages=goods_buy_packages,
        consumption_scales=consumption_scales,
    )

pop_income(state: EconomyState) -> ndarray

Return disposable cooperative and dependent household income.

Each configuration distributes all of its positive building_surplus in proportion to state.pops * wage_weight. Every profession is included regardless of paid_private_wage; zero weights receive no cooperative income. Configurations are independent, including those of the same building type. Losses pay zero cooperative wages and remain visible through state.building_deficit, before any optional operating-loss subsidy. Add pops * dependents_per_worker * dependent_wage / 52 for household dependent earnings; missing annual dependent wages default to zero.

  • ndarray –

Raises:

    If relevant arrays are misaligned or non-finite, prices, populations, or wage weights are negative, profession keys are invalid, wage weights are missing, used dependent wages are invalid, calculated income is non-finite, or a configuration has positive surplus but no positive recipient weight.

Notes

This is a simplified worker-cooperative accounting policy. It applies proportional income tax when context.subsidize_operating_losses is enabled. Losses exceeding total gross income raise ValueError. It excludes transfers, subsistence income, reserves, and household expenses, and does not change wealth or pop_balance. Dependent earnings do not reduce building surplus or increase production GDP.

def pop_income(self, state: EconomyState) -> np.ndarray:
    """Return disposable cooperative and dependent household income.

    Each configuration distributes all of its positive ``building_surplus``
    in proportion to ``state.pops * wage_weight``. Every profession is
    included regardless of ``paid_private_wage``; zero weights receive no
    cooperative income. Configurations are independent, including those of the same
    building type. Losses pay zero cooperative wages and remain visible
    through ``state.building_deficit``, before any optional operating-loss subsidy.
    Add ``pops * dependents_per_worker * dependent_wage / 52`` for household
    dependent earnings; missing annual dependent wages default to zero.

    Args:
        state: Snapshot aligned to this economy's configuration, goods, and
            profession indexes. Stored signed flows and market prices are
            authoritative; production and throughput are not reconstructed.

    Returns:
        A fresh writable float64 matrix shaped like ``state.pops`` containing
        total household income in £ per week for each configuration-profession
        group, rather than per-worker rates. The state and model tables are unchanged.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If relevant arrays are misaligned or non-finite, prices,
            populations, or wage weights are negative, profession keys are
            invalid, wage weights are missing, used dependent wages are invalid,
            calculated income is non-finite, or a configuration has positive
            surplus but no positive recipient weight.

    Notes:
        This is a simplified worker-cooperative accounting policy. It applies
        proportional income tax when context.subsidize_operating_losses is enabled.
        Losses exceeding total gross income raise ValueError. It excludes
        transfers, subsistence income, reserves, and household expenses, and
        does not change wealth or ``pop_balance``. Dependent earnings do not
        reduce building surplus or increase production GDP.
    """
    return _income.pop_income(self, state)
