docs.title: Economy modeling
docs.text:
For calculation dependencies and the owner of each state value, see the economy dependency graphs.

See the production-table dictionary for input coefficients and the economy-report dictionary for exported state columns, formulas, and units.

docs.title: Economy data and alignment
docs.text:
An Economy model uses production, goods, pop-types, pop-needs, and buy-package tables, each represented by a parsed DataFrame in parsing.

You can either construct an Economy from the parsed tables, or let it parse them internally as below:

from vic3_analysis import Economy
economy = Economy()

Immutability

Economy is a frozen dataclass that deep-copies its input tables. Its public DataFrames remain mutable, but editing them is unsupported: construct a new Economy for changed model data, because cached coefficients are not invalidated. Indexes (building_index, goods_index, pop_index, and producible_goods) are cached tuples. Fixed coefficients such as base_prices, employment_matrix, employment_vector, construction_cost_vector, arable_land_vector, infrastructure_vector, and pop_wealth_init are cached, read-only arrays. The components of EconomyState own read-only copies of input arrays. Its realized building_goods_flow matrix has one row per configuration and one column per good, in model index order. Entries are weekly quantities after levels, throughput, and economy-of-scale bonuses: outputs are positive and inputs negative.

To display names while keeping the model's key-based alignment, request a language when parsing the internal tables:

from vic3_analysis import Economy

economy = Economy(language="english")

Localization is added only to internally parsed DataFrames. If df_production, df_goods, df_pop_types, df_pop_needs, or df_buy_packages is supplied explicitly, its contents are copied without adding localization or changing the supplied data.

import numpy as np

unscaled = economy.goods_input_matrix_unscaled
multipliers = np.full(unscaled.shape[0], 2.0)
scaled = economy.goods_input_matrix(throughput_multipliers=multipliers)

The unscaled input and output matrices are prepared together from the production table and cached as separate read-only arrays. Scaled matrices remain writable copies.

Snapshot helpers use the state argument name, including keyword calls such as economy.df_market(state=state) and economy.construction_cost(state=state).

docs.title: Direct solving
docs.text:
Now that we have a model of the economy, if we know the levels of each building, we can solve for all kinds of metrics we care about, such as employment, goods flows, and GDP, all of which stored in the EconomyState dataclass.

import numpy as np
# Assume we have one level of everything
levels = np.ones(len(economy.building_index), dtype=np.float64)
state = economy.solve(levels)
print("Class of the state:", type(state))
print("Annual GDP: ", state.gdp(annual=True))
print("Total employed population: ", state.total_employment)
print("Workers and dependents: ", state.total_population)

Economy.solve() default to nominal mode, which ignores the market price mechanic and uses base prices for each good.

You can also use market mode, which derives national prices from buy and sell orders, just like the game does (still no local prices though).

Pass fixed weekly trade quantities with goods_import and goods_export. Both are non-negative finite 1-D arrays aligned to economy.goods_index, and default to zeros. Imports add sell orders; exports add buy orders. A good may have imports and exports simultaneously; both gross quantities affect prices.

imports = np.zeros(len(economy.goods_index), dtype=np.float64)
exports = np.zeros(len(economy.goods_index), dtype=np.float64)
imports[economy.goods_index.index("tools")] = 5.0
exports[economy.goods_index.index("tools")] = 2.0
state = economy.solve(
    levels, method="market", goods_import=imports, goods_export=exports
)

EconomyContext owns read-only goods_import and goods_export arrays. The state forwards these arrays and exposes imports and exports as aliases. goods_trade_flow is a read-only derived vector of net imports, goods_import - goods_export; market orders use the gross arrays. Optimization scenarios express each trade input as named (good, amount) pairs. Fixed demand assumptions in nominal/market studies can be supplied as export orders. Such orders appear as exports in reports and are separate from calculated household consumption. In equilibrium, exports are additional external demand.

Economy.solve() also supports throughput bonuses via economy of scale and parameterized throughput_multipliers. The two are applied additively to the raw throughput of each building, which is then used to compute goods flows.

Set economy_of_scale_level_cap=20.0 to apply up to +20% economy of scale throughput; leave it at 0.0 to disable the effect.

import numpy as np

levels = np.ones(len(economy.building_index), dtype=np.float64)
state = economy.solve(
    levels,
    method="market",
    throughput_multipliers=np.full(len(economy.building_index), 1.5),
    economy_of_scale_level_cap=20.0
)

To choose building levels from objectives and constraints, continue with the optimization guide. See the economy API for model parameters and state reports.

docs.title: Snapshot components and preparation
docs.text:
All four state classes are available from vic3_analysis:

Component Stored inputs Derived values EconomyContext (state.context) Building levels, realized goods flows, trade, workers, workforce ratio, optional baskets and scales Goods input/output totals, sell orders, non-household buy orders, population totals MarketState (state.market) Shared context reference and prices Building surplus, deficit, and GDP PopState (state.households) Wealth, household demand, optional income and expenses Balance, when both finances are supplied EconomyState References to these three components Total buy orders, wealth statistics, per-capita reports

Existing flat reads such as state.pops and state.market_prices forward to their owning components. Direct construction now uses EconomyState(context=context, market=market, households=households). The market must reference the exact same context object.

Nominal and market solves leave goods_buy_packages, consumption_scales, pop_income, and pop_expenses as None. They continue to accept externally supplied population demand without evaluating household finances. pop_balance is None until both finances exist; df_pop() reports unavailable balances as NaN.

Prepare the fixed consumption inputs explicitly, then share them across snapshots:

from dataclasses import replace
from vic3_analysis import MarketState

context = economy.prepare_context(state.context)
state = replace(
    state,
    context=context,
    market=MarketState(context=context, market_prices=state.market_prices),
)
needs = economy.pop_buy_orders(state)
expenses = economy.pop_expenses(state)

The context stores goods_buy_packages as an immutable GoodsBuyPackages object containing read-only arrays: wealth holds ascending positive integer row labels, and quantities holds the wealth-by-goods matrix. Goods columns follow the owning economy's goods_index; worker columns follow pop_index. goods_buy_packages(context) returns GoodsBuyPackages, reusing the prepared object when present. df_goods_buy_packages(source) exports an independent DataFrame from a state, context, or basket object, while pop_consumption_scales(context) returns an independent writable array. Both calculators also accept complete states.

To supply custom prepared baskets, construct one object with both arrays:

import numpy as np

from vic3_analysis import GoodsBuyPackages

packages = GoodsBuyPackages(
    wealth=np.array([1, 5]),
    quantities=np.zeros((2, len(economy.goods_index))),
)
context = replace(state.context, goods_buy_packages=packages)

GoodsBuyPackages owns copies of its inputs, validates their alignment, and sorts labels and quantities together. Contexts share the immutable object. Use context.goods_buy_packages.wealth and context.goods_buy_packages.quantities after checking that baskets are prepared. This replaces the former separate buy_packages array and buy_package_wealth attributes.

prepare_context() computes only missing fields, returning the original context when fully prepared. Needs and expenses resolve baskets and scales independently: explicit arguments take precedence, then prepared context values, then calculation. No household-by-goods tensor is retained.

Refresh baskets when production, trade, or substitution assumptions change. Refresh scales when workers, workforce ratio, or profession multipliers change. For example, changing the workforce ratio requires clearing the old scales:

context = economy.prepare_context(
    replace(state.context, workforce_ratio=0.25, consumption_scales=None)
)
state = replace(state, context=context, market=replace(state.market, context=context))

Set goods_buy_packages=None when refreshing baskets. Wealth and prices may change while sharing the same context. Context preparation does not evaluate wealth or implement iteration.

docs.title: Workers and dependents
docs.text:
EconomyState.pops always stores employed workers. Set the economy-wide workforce_ratio to the worker share of total population; it defaults to 1.0 to preserve worker-only accounting. The ratio must be finite and in (0, 1].

state = economy.solve(levels, method="market", workforce_ratio=0.25)
print(state.dependents_per_worker)  # 3.0, a cached property
print(state.total_employment)      # workers
print(state.total_population)      # four times the workers

Dependents are derived without another population matrix. They share each worker group's profession and wealth, consume half as much per person, and earn the profession's annual dependent_wage divided by 52 per week. For 100 workers at a ratio of 0.25, there are 300 dependents, 400 people, and 250 standard-worker equivalents of consumption before profession consumption multipliers.

GDP per capita divides production GDP by workers plus dependents. Total wealth weights wealth tiers by all people; averages, wealth distributions, Gini, and profession shares are unchanged by a uniform ratio. df_pop() reports separate employment, dependents, and population counts. Unemployed workers and demographic transitions are not inferred.

docs.title: Building flows and cooperative income
docs.text:
state.building_goods_input and state.building_goods_output are cached, read-only totals derived from state.building_goods_flow. Signs are split before summing configurations, so a good produced by one configuration and consumed by another contributes to both sell and buy orders. The matrix retains the production table's signed net coefficients within each configuration; it does not recover gross inputs offset by outputs of the same good within a row.

Realized flows belong to EconomyContext. When changing an existing state, replace its context and rebind the market to the new context. Clear prepared baskets because the changed flows affect substitution:

from dataclasses import replace

context = replace(
    state.context,
    building_goods_flow=state.building_goods_flow * 2,
    goods_buy_packages=None,
)
changed_state = replace(state, context=context, market=replace(state.market, context=context))

state.building_surplus is each configuration's weekly goods value added at the state's prices, before wages. state.building_deficit is the positive magnitude of a negative surplus, representing input costs not covered by output revenue. Both are cached, read-only arrays aligned to building_index. Replacing flows or prices creates a new state with fresh caches.

pop_income(state) implements a simplified worker-cooperative policy: each configuration distributes all positive surplus to its employees in proportion to employee counts times profession wage_weight. Every employed profession participates regardless of paid_private_wage; zero weights receive zero cooperative income. Configurations of the same building type distribute independently.

state = economy.solve(levels, method="market")
income = economy.pop_income(state)
income_by_profession = income.sum(axis=0)
deficits_by_configuration = state.building_deficit

The returned writable float64 matrix matches state.pops.shape and records household totals in pounds per week, rather than per-worker income. It uses stored flows and prices directly, so no throughput arguments are needed. Loss-making configurations pay zero wages and retain an unfunded deficit. A positive surplus without any positive recipient weight raises ValueError identifying the configuration. Missing, negative, or non-finite wage weights are also errors.

Dependent earnings are added as pops * dependents_per_worker * dependent_wage / 52; missing wages mean zero. Only coefficients used by represented dependents are validated. These exogenous earnings do not reduce building surplus or increase production GDP, and remain available when a workplace has a loss.

The calculation leaves the state and pop_balance unchanged. Nominal and market solves do not automatically calculate income. Equilibrium funds operating losses through the income tax described below by default. Setting subsidize_operating_losses=False disables that tax. The model excludes other transfers, reserves, and subsistence income.

docs.title: Population needs
docs.text:
pop_buy_orders(state) returns weekly goods quantities aligned to goods_index. It uses the state's employed-worker counts and integer wealth, the model's df_buy_packages, and the goods substitution definitions in df_pop_needs. Both tables can be passed as keyword arguments when constructing Economy; omitted tables are parsed from the game files.

from dataclasses import replace
from vic3_analysis import EconomyState

state = economy.solve(levels)
needs = economy.pop_buy_orders(state)
state_with_needs = replace(state, households=replace(state.households, pop_buy_orders=needs))
# Evaluate demand, prices, and household finances at the state's fixed wealth:
market, households = economy.evaluate_wealth(state.context, state.pop_wealth)
market_state = EconomyState(market.context, market, households)

solve() in nominal/market mode leaves household demand at zero. evaluate_wealth() calculates demand and prices at fixed wealth; equilibrium solving also iterates wealth. The calculation leaves the supplied state unchanged. pop_wealth and pop_wealth_init are read-only int64 arrays; integer-valued floating inputs are accepted, while fractional, negative, non-finite, or overflowing wealth is rejected. Occupied wealth levels must have a buy package. Empty cells can use zero or other undefined integer wealth levels.

For each need, effective supply is sell orders minus half of building and export demand, clamped to zero. Goods' shares of that supply are clipped to their configured minimum and maximum, multiplied by their weights, and then normalized. These limits apply before normalization, so a final purchase share can exceed its configured maximum supply share. Minimum shares can generate demand for absent goods; if all purchase weights are zero, the default good receives the whole category's demand.

Wealth packages specify category values at base prices per 10,000 workers. Values are scaled by employment * (1 + 0.5 * dependents_per_worker) and profession consumption_mult (default 1, with peasants normally consuming 0.05), allocated by purchase weights, and divided by each good's base price. Existing population demand and market prices do not affect the calculation. Cultural modifiers, prestige goods, local-state effects, weekly adjustment, and wealth feedback are not modeled here.

docs.title: Standard packages by wealth
docs.text:
goods_buy_packages(state) returns immutable GoodsBuyPackages of weekly goods quantities per 10,000 standard workers. Its read-only wealth array contains ascending positive int64 labels, and quantities is a read-only float64 matrix with columns in goods_index order and zeros for unconsumed goods. Prepared context baskets are authoritative and reused; otherwise every level defined in the raw df_buy_packages table is calculated.

packages = economy.goods_buy_packages(state)
wealth = int(packages.wealth[0])
goods_at_wealth = packages.quantities[0]
# Convert only when a table or export is needed:
report = economy.df_goods_buy_packages(packages)

The packages use the state's building inputs/outputs, imports, and exports for goods substitution. They do not depend on population counts, occupied wealth levels, profession consumption multipliers, market prices, or existing population demand. Even an empty population has a complete set of calculated baskets. Each row's value at base prices equals its wealth tier's total category budget. The returned object owns read-only arrays. df_goods_buy_packages(state), df_goods_buy_packages(context), or df_goods_buy_packages(packages) returns an independently mutable report with int64 index named wealth and goods columns in model order. Editing that report changes no baskets or model tables.

Pass the basket object to pop_buy_orders to reuse its goods quantities:

packages = economy.goods_buy_packages(state)
needs = economy.pop_buy_orders(state, goods_buy_packages=packages)
next_state = economy.solve(
    levels, method="market", throughput_multipliers=np.full(len(levels), 1.1)
)
next_needs = economy.pop_buy_orders(next_state, goods_buy_packages=packages)

Supplied baskets stay fixed when market supply changes. Demand is calculated directly from each occupied wealth tier's goods quantities, scaled by worker- equivalent counts including half-rate dependent consumption, and profession consumption multipliers per 10,000 workers. Substitution, base-price conversion, and validation of unused state goods flows and raw need/package tables are skipped.

GoodsBuyPackages construction validates unique positive integer wealth labels and finite nonnegative quantities, and sorts rows with their labels. Quantity columns must already follow the model's goods_index order; consumption calculations check the column count and coverage of occupied tiers. Only occupied wealth tiers need rows; empty population cells need no matching package. Explicit baskets, prepared context baskets, and freshly calculated baskets use the same selection path. DataFrames are not accepted as basket arguments. The basket object and state remain unchanged.

docs.title: Reusable household consumption scales
docs.text:
pop_consumption_scales(state) returns a fresh writable float64 matrix aligned to configurations × professions. Each cell is a dimensionless multiple of a weekly basket for 10,000 standard workers:

scale = workers / 10_000 * consumption_mult * (1 + 0.5 * dependents_per_worker)

Missing profession multipliers default to 1. Scales are independent of wealth, market prices, and goods flows. Reuse scales while worker counts, workforce ratio, and profession multipliers remain unchanged. Reuse the basket table while production, trade, and substitution assumptions remain unchanged; both can be reused after changing household wealth or market prices.

Pass either or both precomputed inputs to needs and expense calculations:

packages = economy.goods_buy_packages(state)
scales = economy.pop_consumption_scales(state)
needs = economy.pop_buy_orders(
    state, goods_buy_packages=packages, consumption_scales=scales
)
expenses = economy.pop_expenses(
    state, goods_buy_packages=packages, consumption_scales=scales
)
income = economy.pop_income(state)
balance = income - expenses

Supplied scales are authoritative: they must match state.pops.shape, contain finite nonnegative values, and be zero wherever worker counts are zero. They already include all population factors, which are not reapplied or checked against the current profession multipliers or workforce ratio. The caller is responsible for refreshing stale scales. Omitted scales reuse prepared context scales when present, otherwise calling pop_consumption_scales(state). Every occupied wealth tier needs a basket even if its scale is zero; empty cells need no defined wealth tier.

docs.title: Household expenses
docs.text:
pop_expenses(state) returns a fresh writable float64 matrix shaped like state.pops, containing household consumption expenses in pounds per week. It values each occupied wealth tier's goods basket at state.market_prices and multiplies by its consumption scale, including profession and dependent effects. Prices must be finite, nonnegative, and goods-aligned; zero prices are valid. Changing prices changes expenses without changing basket quantities.

The goods_buy_packages argument follows the same contract as for needs. Supplied baskets bypass unused production flows, base prices, and raw needs/package tables. Empty households have zero expenses; an empty population may use an empty supplied basket table. All calculated costs and expenses must be finite.

With matching baskets and scales, total expenses equal needs @ state.market_prices. The methods aggregate quantities by wealth tier and do not allocate a configuration-by-profession-by-goods tensor. They leave the state, supplied arrays/tables, and model tables unchanged. In particular, balance above is calculated explicitly; state.pop_balance is unchanged. Store finances explicitly to obtain a derived balance on a new snapshot:

state = replace(
    state,
    households=replace(state.households, pop_income=income, pop_expenses=expenses),
)
balance = state.pop_balance  # Read-only income minus expenses.

Replacing just the market or household component shares state.context and its production arrays. The caller must refresh dependent results when changing wealth or prices; constructing a snapshot does not recalculate demand or finances. Expenses price target consumption without affordability limits, rationing, taxes, or wealth transitions. Nominal and market modes do not automatically calculate expenses or balances.

docs.title: Evaluating fixed wealth
docs.text:
evaluate_wealth(context, pop_wealth) evaluates one wealth assignment and returns matching market and household components. It calls prepare_context() to fill missing baskets and consumption scales, preserving any supplied prepared fields. It then calculates household goods demand, derives market prices from industrial, export, and household buy orders against production and import sell orders, and evaluates cooperative income and household expenses at those same prices.

initial = economy.solve(building_levels, workforce_ratio=0.25)
market, households = economy.evaluate_wealth(initial.context, initial.pop_wealth)
state = EconomyState(market.context, market, households)
balance = state.pop_balance  # Evaluated, read-only weekly income minus expenses.

Use market.context when composing the result: it is the supplied context when already fully prepared, or a newly prepared context otherwise. Inputs and model tables remain unchanged. Returned arrays are read-only, and supplied wealth values are preserved as int64. Wealth must match configurations × professions; every occupied tier needs a basket, including households with zero consumption scales. Empty cells may use undefined nonnegative integer tiers.

Total household expenses equal households.pop_buy_orders @ market.market_prices within floating-point precision. Existing preparation, input validation, and income-allocation errors propagate. This evaluates target consumption without affordability limits or wealth transitions; nominal and market solve modes continue to leave household finances unevaluated.

docs.title: Iterating wealth
docs.text:
Initialize matching components, then take one simultaneous step:

market, households = economy.evaluate_wealth(initial.context, initial.pop_wealth)
context = market.context
market, households = economy.iterate(context, market, households)
state = EconomyState(context, market, households)

iterate() trusts the supplied components' economic consistency. It requires evaluated income and expenses, a market referencing the exact same context, and prepared baskets/scales. Reevaluate after externally changing wealth, production, or trade. Prepared wealth labels must be consecutive; occupied wealth must be covered. Empty cells retain their original wealth labels.

Using previous prices and income, each occupied household decreases one tier when income is below 98% of its current-tier cost. Otherwise, it increases one tier when income reaches 102% of its next-tier cost. Other households retain their tier. Decreases take precedence even if basket costs are nonmonotonic. These constants follow WEALTH_PROGRESS_ACCEPTABLE_DEFICIT and WEALTH_PROGRESS_WANTED_BUFFER in the local game's common/defines/00_defines.txt. The steps are numerical; weekly wealth-progress timing is not simulated.

For a threshold B, comparisons use t = atol + rtol * max(abs(income), abs(B)): decrease when income < B - t, advance when income >= B - t. Defaults are rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-8; zero tolerances recover exact comparisons. Costs and income are weekly totals for each configuration/profession household group. At the minimum tier, downward movement is suppressed; at the maximum tier, advancement is omitted. If nothing changes, iterate() returns the supplied objects. Otherwise, it evaluates the new assignment once and returns matching read-only components sharing the fixed context.

docs.title: Solving equilibrium
docs.text:
from vic3_analysis import EquilibriumError

try:
    state = economy.solve(
        building_levels,
        method="equilibrium",
        workforce_ratio=0.25,
        max_iterations=1000,
        # initial_wealth=previous_state.pop_wealth,  # Optional full-matrix warm start.
    )
except EquilibriumError as error:
    last_state = error.state
    print(error.diagnostics.status, error.diagnostics.iterations)
    print(error.diagnostics.increasing_cells, error.diagnostics.decreasing_cells)
else:
    diagnostics = state.equilibrium_diagnostics
    print(diagnostics)

Equilibrium prepares fixed production, trade, baskets, consumption scales, cooperative allocation shares, and dependent earnings once. The solver then iterates wealth, demand, prices, income, and expenses. initial_wealth defaults to profession starting tiers, or accepts a nonnegative integer matrix matching configurations × professions. Unsupported occupied tiers are rejected rather than clipped. Household demand is calculated endogenously, alongside any fixed import and export orders.

Success requires no permitted wealth changes and a fresh final verification through the accounting calculators. An initially stable assignment reports zero iterations. max_iterations is a positive integer counting completed transition steps; initialization and final verification do not count. Convergence and cycles are checked at the final allowed step before exhaustion is reported.

state.equilibrium_diagnostics.status == "converged" describes stationary wealth. It can coexist with unaffordable_floor_cells or loss_buildings. The former identifies households below their lower affordability threshold at the minimum tier. The latter identifies unfunded losses larger than atol + rtol * max(output_value, input_value), using the existing signed-flow accounting. Unfunded loss flags can accompany a successful solve when subsidize_operating_losses=False. Dependent earnings remain exogenous, and trade remains fixed orders.

docs.title: Tax-funded operating losses
docs.text:
Equilibrium covers every configuration's operating loss through a proportional tax on all represented household income by default:

state = economy.solve(levels, method="equilibrium")
gross_income = state.pop_income_before_tax
tax = state.pop_income_tax
disposable_income = state.pop_income

At each price evaluation, total subsidy cost is D = state.building_deficit.sum(). Gross income Y includes both cooperative surplus distributions and dependent earnings. Every household pays the same rate D / Y.sum(); zero-income households pay zero. No losses means zero tax, including for an empty economy. Subsidies pay building costs directly; they add no payroll or household transfer. Wealth transitions and balances use disposable income, and taxes are recomputed when prices change. GDP still measures production value added; it is not reduced again by the subsidy transfer.

building_surplus and building_deficit continue to describe production before subsidies. Funded losses do not appear in diagnostic loss_buildings. pop_income_tax and derived pop_income_before_tax are read-only matrices aligned to pops. Evaluated untaxed states have zero tax arrays; unevaluated finances remain None. economy.pop_income(state) and economy.pop_income_tax(state) recompute the policy from the stored context and prices.

Exactly 100% tax is allowed. Losses exceeding all gross income raise EquilibriumError with status insufficient_income, including at initialization. Its snapshot contains the failing wealth and prices, gross income in pop_income, and zero tax collected; it is not a successful funded state. Direct income calculation and evaluate_wealth() instead raise ValueError. A failure during iteration retains the failing evaluation rather than the preceding funded one.

Disable the policy with subsidize_operating_losses=False. Direct EconomyContext construction and equilibrium optimizers also default to enabled. The context retains the selected policy for evaluate_wealth() and iterate(). Economy.solve() resolves an omitted or None policy to enabled for equilibrium and disabled for nominal/market modes. Explicitly enabling it for nominal or market modes is rejected.

EquilibriumError distinguishes cycle, max_iterations, evaluation_failed, verification_failed, and insufficient_income. Its immutable .state retains the last complete evaluation and references the same .diagnostics. Diagnostics identify cells requiring changes and financial flags; cycles additionally report cycle_start and cycle_length. Household coordinates are (configuration_index, profession_index) in economy index order; building flags are configuration indices. Calculation failures chain their original exception as __cause__. Invalid setup or initial evaluations other than insufficient income raise ValueError directly. A detected cycle or exhausted budget does not prove that no equilibrium exists.

Nominal and market modes retain their existing behavior and leave equilibrium diagnostics as None; equilibrium controls are ignored in those modes.

For concise live diagnostics, enable the standard logger vic3_analysis.analysis.economy.equilibrium at DEBUG. It reports solver start, completed wealth transitions, elapsed seconds, success/failure status, cycle information on failure, and financial-flag counts on success. An iteration summary appears after initialization (inner_iterations=0) and after each completed wealth transition. It counts cells eligible to increase or decrease wealth, unaffordable floor cells, and loss-making building configurations. The increase/decrease counts describe changes permitted from the current assignment, rather than changes already applied. Verification-started and verification-completed events bracket successful final verification; failure is reported by the existing solver failure summary. Library code does not configure handlers; see logging configuration and optimizer progress.

docs.title: Exporting standard packages
docs.text:
To export packages for an economy with no buildings, run examples/buy_packages.py from the repository root:

uv run python examples/buy_packages.py
# Equivalent module invocation:
uv run python -m examples.buy_packages

The example parses the local game installation directly, without requiring previously exported parser tables. Initialize the artifact checkout first with git submodule update --init --recursive if necessary. It constructs an EconomyState with zero building levels, production, imports, exports, and represented employment. Standard packages remain defined for all wealth tiers: with zero supply, minimum shares apply, and categories with zero purchase weights fall back to their default goods.

The example calls economy.df_goods_buy_packages(state) for the DataFrame export. The UTF-8 output is artifacts/analyses/buy_packages/default.csv, with wealth as the first column followed by goods in model order. Re-running the example replaces this CSV, and the script prints its output path.

The method's docstring links the game definitions, the Needs formulas, and the official developer diary. The half-non-pop-demand deduction comes from community reverse engineering documented by the wiki; zero-clamping effective supply is a model convention.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Set up the package, then choose a guide for the analysis you want to run.

docs.title: Prepare the checkout
docs.text:
Clone the repository and install its locked development environment:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/ShabbyGayBar/victoria3-analysis.git
cd victoria3-analysis
uv sync

For an existing checkout, initialize the pinned artifact submodule with git submodule update --init --recursive. The examples require this artifact checkout. Generate parsed datasets first, then the production table, then study results; see the parsing guide for commands and output paths.

docs.title: Continue from here
docs.text:
• Parse your installed game to refresh the source tables.
  • Model economies and evaluate building levels directly.
  • Optimize production with objectives and constraints.
  • Trace supply chains and compare scenarios.
  • Browse every generated result and its runnable script.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
Mathematical Programming is the foundation of analyzing and optimizing Victoria 3's economy. The vic3_analysis package provides optimizers that choose building levels, which maximize or minimize the objective, for an Economy according to a scenario's constraints. Start with an economy model:

from vic3_analysis import Economy

economy = Economy()

See the economy guide for model construction and direct solving, and the economy-report dictionary for returned state columns, formulas, and units.

docs.title: Scenario definition
docs.text:
Objective and constraints are defined in an immutable Scenario dataclass. Create a new scenario to change its assumptions.

  • Use game script keys when setting attributes of Scenario, such as "steel" or "building_steel_mills", rather than localized display names.
  • Fields containing pairs use tuples such as (("steel", 100.0),)
  • Fields containing only keys use tuples such as ("pm_diesel_engines",).
  • An empty tuple () adds no entries.
  • Optional caps default to None, which leaves that constraint disabled.
  • The decision variables are non-negative, continuous (Fractional levels are allowed) building levels for each production configuration.
  • Use weekly flows when setting goods quantities
  • Employment is the workforce headcount, excluding dependents.

docs.title: Scenario name
docs.text: Attribute Default Meaning name None Optional label for the experiment; it does not affect the solution. display_name() returns this label, otherwise joins the unique goods_export good keys in first-occurrence order with +, or returns "unnamed" when there are no exports.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The objective attribute defaults to "automation". Its supported values are:

Objective Direction Meaning Optimizer gdp maximize Model GDP: net goods output valued at base prices with NominalOptimizer, or endogenous market prices with MarketOptimizer and EquilibriumOptimizer. All three gdp_per_capita maximize Market-price GDP divided by workers plus dependents. Market and equilibrium average_wealth maximize Population-weighted household wealth tier, equal to employment-weighted wealth under the uniform workforce ratio. Equilibrium only employment maximize Total employed population. Nominal only automation minimize Employment required to satisfy the constraints. Nominal only construction_cost minimize Total construction cost required to satisfy the constraints. Nominal only

docs.title: Goods balance and market orders
docs.text:
Attribute Default Meaning min_goods_balance 0.0 Minimum weekly balance for every good: building output + imports − building inputs − exports. Household consumption is excluded. Zero prevents deficits, negative values permit bounded deficits, and None disables the constraint. Numeric floors must be finite. goods_import () Fixed weekly non-negative (good, amount) pairs adding sell orders. Imports allow domestic production deficits under the balance floor and affect market prices. goods_export () Fixed weekly non-negative (good, amount) pairs adding buy orders. With a zero balance floor, production plus imports must cover building inputs and exports. workforce_ratio 1.0 Uniform workers / total population in (0, 1], retained in returned states. Employment caps count workers. Market GDP per capita and its gradient scale by this ratio; equilibrium also uses it for dependent consumption and earnings.

goods_import and goods_export require known good keys and finite, non-negative amounts. Repeated entries for the same good are summed within each input. A good may have both import and export orders, which are kept separate when calculating prices. Orders are fixed, rather than optimized. They enter the balance constraints in every optimizer when the floor is enabled. Market and equilibrium optimizers also use them to calculate prices. Household demand affects equilibrium prices but is excluded from the balance floor.

For example, with min_goods_balance=0.0, goods_import=(("steel", 20.0),) permits domestic steel production to fall 20 units below building consumption each week. Conversely, goods_export=(("steel", 100.0),) requires at least 100 units of net domestic steel output when no steel is imported. With both orders, the net domestic requirement is 80 units. A floor of 5 raises that requirement to 85 units.

docs.title: Available configurations and throughput
docs.text:
Attribute Default Meaning banned_pms () Production-method keys to exclude. Every production configuration containing any listed method is forced to zero levels. banned_building_groups () Building-group keys to exclude. Configurations whose building_group exactly matches a listed key are forced to zero; parent-group descendants are not matched automatically. era_cap None Highest permitted technology era. Configurations whose production-table era exceeds this value are forced to zero levels. Requires an era-enriched production table. throughput_multipliers () (building, multiplier) pairs applied to every configuration of that building. 1.5 means 150% throughput (+50%). Gross goods inputs and outputs both scale; employment and construction cost per level do not. Repeated entries for one building multiply together.

All optimizers disable level-dependent economy-of-scale bonuses. Use fixed throughput_multipliers to represent throughput assumptions in the scenario.

docs.title: Capacity and relationship constraints
docs.text: Attribute Default Meaning building_level_caps () (building, maximum_levels) pairs capping the sum of levels across all configurations of that building. A zero limit bans the building. State-region resource helpers produce limits in this form. construction_cost_cap None Maximum total construction points: the sum of building levels multiplied by each configuration's construction_cost. employment_cap None Maximum total employed population: the sum of building levels multiplied by per-level employment. arable_land_cap None Maximum total arable-land use. Each level in the model's agricultural, plantation, ranching, or subsistence land-use groups consumes one unit; other configurations consume zero. min_net_infrastructure None Minimum total infrastructure generation minus consumption, weighted by building levels. Net infrastructure is the negative of the production-table infrastructure_usage_per_level total; missing values are treated as zero. 0.0 prevents deficits, positive values require spare capacity, and negative values permit a bounded deficit. None leaves infrastructure unconstrained. urbanization_per_center None Urbanization points required per level of building_urban_center. Enforces an equality: total building urbanization equals this value multiplied by total urban-center levels. For example, 100.0 ties each center level to 100 urbanization points.

docs.title: Example scenario
docs.text:
from vic3_analysis import NominalOptimizer, Scenario

scenario = Scenario(
    goods_export=(("automobiles", 100.0),),
    objective="automation",
    min_goods_balance=0.0,
    era_cap=5,
    banned_pms=("pm_diesel_engines",),
)
state = NominalOptimizer(economy).solve(scenario)

docs.title: Problem inspection and solving
docs.text:
Use optimizer.compile(scenario) to inspect the resulting compiled problem before solving it, or optimizer.solve_problem(problem) to solve an already compiled problem. Shared context and constraints are compiled by BaseOptimizer; Scenario remains configuration-only.

After solving, call optimizer.summary() for a fresh one-row DataFrame of scenario settings, economy metrics, and search diagnostics:

optimizer = NominalOptimizer(economy)
state = optimizer.solve(scenario)
summary = optimizer.summary()

The report includes weekly and annual GDP, annual GDP per capita, worker employment, total population including dependents, average wealth tier, construction cost, arable-land consumption, and net infrastructure usage (consumption minus generation). throughput_multiplier contains the common compiled multiplier, or NaN when configuration multipliers differ. Level-dependent economy-of-scale bonuses remain disabled.

Equilibrium optimizers add household convergence diagnostics and evaluation counts; the supply-chain optimizer also reports chain and building configuration counts. A budget-limited search that returns a verified equilibrium can be summarized with search_success=False. Reporting uses the retained solution without rerunning the solver. Calling summary() before a solution is returned, after binding a new problem, or after solving or verifying that bound problem fails raises ValueError. Each report is independent and can be extended with experiment metadata using summary.assign(...).

For endogenous national prices, use MarketOptimizer. It supports gdp and gdp_per_capita and accepts numeric min_goods_balance floors or None. Fixed goods_import and goods_export orders affect prices and enter enabled goods-balance constraints. Its SLSQP solve is local and requires a bounded scenario. The model excludes shortages, MAPI and local prices, wealth feedback, endogenous demand, and economy-of-scale bonuses.

from vic3_analysis import MarketOptimizer, Scenario

scenario = Scenario(
    goods_export=(("automobiles", 100.0),),
    objective="gdp_per_capita",
    min_goods_balance=0.0,
    employment_cap=1_000_000.0,
)
state = MarketOptimizer(economy).solve(scenario)

docs.title: Equilibrium optimization
docs.text:
For a runnable example and saved building levels, see the million-worker wealth search.

EquilibriumOptimizer chooses building levels while the existing household equilibrium solver determines wealth, consumption, prices, and finances. It supports gdp, gdp_per_capita, and average_wealth. Population varies with employment; an employment cap does not require the optimizer to employ everyone.

from vic3_analysis import EquilibriumOptimizer, Scenario

scenario = Scenario(
    objective="average_wealth",
    min_goods_balance=None,
    workforce_ratio=0.25,
    building_level_caps=tuple(
        (str(building), 100.0)
        for building in economy.df_production["building"].unique()
    ),
)
optimizer = EquilibriumOptimizer(economy)
problem = optimizer.compile(scenario, max_iterations=1000)
state = optimizer.solve_problem(problem, options={"maxiter": 20_000})
print(state.average_wealth, state.gdp_per_capita(annual=True))
print(optimizer.result.success, optimizer.result.message)
print(optimizer.result.equilibrium_failures)

The linear scenario region must be feasible and bounded. Capping every building is one way to ensure boundedness. Shared constraints apply to each candidate's building levels, with fixed trade and throughput assumptions. EquilibriumOptimizer permits any min_goods_balance setting.

Equilibrium optimization funds operating losses with a proportional tax on all household income, including dependent earnings, by default. Pass subsidize_operating_losses=False to compile() or solve() to disable it. Compiled problems retain the policy for every evaluation and final verification. Both EquilibriumOptimizer and SupplyChainEquilibriumOptimizer support it. Trials whose operating losses exceed all household income are rejected and counted as insufficient_income failures. These trials receive a finite penalty based on the unfunded fraction of their operating losses. Smaller shortfalls score better, guiding search toward a fundable mix even when the starting point fails. Every such penalty remains worse than every converged objective score. Failed snapshots are never eligible as returned solutions, and trial budgets and final verification still apply. The tax lowers disposable income used for wealth and demand; objective formulas are unchanged. There is no guaranteed payroll. See tax-funded operating losses.

Household consumption is calculated endogenously, while goods_import and goods_export specify fixed external orders.

EquilibriumProblem exposes read-only matrices, named constraint slices, a nominal GDP warm_start LP, evaluate(levels) returning a verified state, and objective(levels) returning its negative, unscaled objective value. Direct evaluation validates physical levels but does not enforce scenario constraints. solve() compiles and solves in one call with the same controls.

Each evaluation rebuilds supply-dependent consumption baskets and starts from the same initial_wealth matrix, defaulting to profession starting tiers. This prevents evaluation order from selecting different wealth histories. An explicit seed must match configurations × professions; it is defensively copied. max_iterations=1000, rtol=1e-9, and atol=1e-8 control the inner equilibrium solver and are frozen in the compiled problem. Empty-population GDP per capita and average wealth remain zero.

The outer search uses deterministic COBYLA local search without derivatives. Wealth tiers can cause jumps and plateaus, so search termination does not certify a global optimum or smooth-objective stationarity. A supplied x0 must satisfy the scenario; otherwise the nominal GDP LP supplies a start. Fixed-zero configurations are removed from search coordinates, and every returned array still follows the full economy index order. Free coordinates are scaled by max(1, abs(starting_level)). Constraint rows are normalized by 1 + abs(rhs); feasibility is independently checked in original units with the existing 1e-7 * (1 + abs(rhs)) tolerance.

Solver options default to maxiter=20_000, rhobeg=1, tol=1e-4, catol=1e-7, and disp=0. maxiter is a hard trial-evaluation budget, including initialization and physically rejected trials. An immediately repeated point reuses the preceding score. Fresh verification of the winner does not consume this budget. Full vanilla searches can take tens of minutes or longer; use a smaller budget for exploration. f_target, when supplied, uses the internal minimizing score: arctan(-metric / scale), where scale is at least one and is fixed from the first converged trial's metric magnitude. The bounded transform preserves metric ordering and gives rejected trials a strictly worse finite penalty. problem.objective() and result.fun retain unscaled units.

EquilibriumError trial outcomes are rejected and counted by status while search continues. Invalid model inputs and unexpected calculation errors propagate. Stationary states with loss_buildings or unaffordable_floor_cells remain valid results under the existing accounting policy; no sustainability constraint, subsidy, or financing model is added.

The optimizer retains the best feasible converged state and independently reevaluates it before returning. Budget exhaustion returns that state with optimizer.result.success == False and an explicit message. Always inspect search status separately from state.equilibrium_diagnostics.status, which must be "converged" on a returned state. Other ordinary COBYLA termination statuses also remain visible on the result.

result.x and result.fun match the returned state. result.nfev counts trial evaluations; result.equilibrium_evaluations counts inner attempts; result.equilibrium_failures maps failure statuses to counts; and result.last_equilibrium_error retains the last failed inner snapshot. result.solver_result retains raw COBYLA output, or None when COBYLA was skipped or interrupted by the hard budget. Working memory retains only the best state, the last failure, and the preceding score. If no feasible converged state is found, solving raises ValueError with these diagnostics still available on .result. A failure during final verification propagates and marks the retained result unsuccessful.

docs.title: Live progress logging
docs.text:
The library uses standard Python module loggers and leaves handler configuration to the caller. Calls remain quiet under Python's default logging levels. Enable INFO summaries and choose a positive trial interval with log_every on either solve() or solve_problem():

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s",
)
state = optimizer.solve_problem(
    problem, log_every=100, options={"maxiter": 20_000}
)

The logger vic3_analysis.optimize.equilibrium reports start, completed preflight and warm start, initialization, periodic progress, search termination, verification, and completion. Periodic summaries appear every log_every uncached trials; lifecycle and terminal messages appear regardless of that interval. COBYLA initialization can consume many trials before its first trust-region iteration. phase=initialization distinguishes this stage from phase=search, which begins when COBYLA reports a trust-region step.

Progress messages contain these scalar fields:

Field Meaning phase, status, message Current stage, run/termination status, and explanatory text. The search stop is logged before fresh verification. trials, elapsed_s Uncached trials used versus the hard budget, and elapsed monotonic seconds since optimizer start. Time includes preflight and verification; trial counts exclude final verification. objective, units, current, best Actual maximizing metric for the latest converged trial and best feasible converged trial. Units are GBP/week, GBP/person/week, or wealth_tier. n/a means no corresponding value is available. These values are unscaled and do not use the internal minimizing transform. current_feasible Whether the latest converged trial satisfies scenario constraints. Physical rejections report False; unverified equilibrium failures report None. A current metric can exceed the best when the current trial is infeasible. feasible_trials, infeasible_trials Counts of converged trial evaluations satisfying or violating the scenario, respectively. Repeated points do not count again. physical_rejections, equilibrium_evaluations Physically invalid trials rejected before an inner solve, and inner solve attempts. failures Counts of skipped equilibrium errors by solver status. Each skipped error remains separate from converged infeasible points. last_equilibrium, last_inner_iterations Latest trial's household outcome and completed wealth-transition count, or None when unavailable. This inner count is separate from optimizer trials.

DEBUG adds individual uncached trial outcomes and new-incumbent messages. The solver logger vic3_analysis.analysis.economy.equilibrium emits DEBUG start, completion, and failure summaries, including completed transitions, cycle information on failure, and financial-flag counts on success. It also emits an iteration summary after initialization (inner_iterations=0) and each completed wealth transition, with counts of cells eligible to increase or decrease wealth, unaffordable floor cells, and loss-making building configurations. Increase/decrease counts describe changes permitted from the current assignment, rather than changes already applied. Verification-started and verification-completed events bracket successful final verification; verification errors appear in the solver failure summary. All of these events remain at DEBUG inside optimizer trials, and household arrays are not logged. Enable that logger independently when using Economy.solve(..., method="equilibrium") directly:

logging.getLogger("vic3_analysis.analysis.economy.equilibrium").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

The final optimizer message distinguishes status=budget_exhausted from household_equilibrium=converged. If verification or another computation fails, it logs the failing phase with status=failed and preserves the original exception. No progress history is retained. Reporting controls are runtime arguments rather than scenario or compiled-problem data; they do not affect the numerical stopping rules, returned metrics, or evaluation budget. Native COBYLA options["disp"] remains available independently.

To save package logs, configure a file handler or pass filename and encoding="utf-8" to logging.basicConfig() in the calling application.

docs.title: State-region limits
docs.text:
from vic3_analysis import (
    StateRegionsParser,
    state_region_arable_land_limit,
    state_region_resource_limits,
)

regions = StateRegionsParser().to_dataframe()
keys = ("STATE_KANTO", "STATE_KANSAI")
limits = state_region_resource_limits(regions, keys)
land = state_region_arable_land_limit(regions, keys)

scenario = Scenario(
    objective="gdp",
    min_goods_balance=0.0,
    building_level_caps=tuple(limits.items()),
    arable_land_cap=land,
)

See the optimization API and resource-limited optimization showcase for a complete regional experiment.

docs.title: Equilibrium optimization over supply chains
docs.text:
SupplyChainEquilibriumOptimizer searches nonnegative chain levels z using fixed recipes supplied as a DataFrame C with building configurations as rows and chains as columns. Every trial computes x = C @ z and passes those building levels to the existing equilibrium solver.

import numpy as np
from vic3_analysis import Scenario, SupplyChainEquilibriumOptimizer, sweep_supply_chains

sweep = sweep_supply_chains(
    economy,
    Scenario(objective="construction_cost"),
    goods=["clothes", "furniture"],
)
optimizer = SupplyChainEquilibriumOptimizer(economy, sweep.df_building_levels)
problem = optimizer.compile(scenario)
state = optimizer.solve_problem(problem, x0=np.ones(len(optimizer.chain_index)))
chain_levels = optimizer.result.x
building_levels = optimizer.to_building_levels(chain_levels)

DataFrame rows identify building configurations and columns identify chains. Rows are aligned by label to economy.building_index; the set of configurations must match exactly. Columns retain their order, except that entirely NaN columns from failed sweep solves are skipped with a UserWarning naming them. No usable columns, partially missing values, negative or nonfinite coefficients, and all-zero recipes raise ValueError. Chain vectors follow the surviving optimizer.chain_index.

The optimizer snapshots read-only coefficients and unique, nonempty string labels. SupplyChainEquilibriumOptimizer.validate_building_levels(frame, building_index=economy.building_index) returns an aligned, independent DataFrame using the same validation. optimizer.df_building_levels returns a defensive copy of the accepted recipes. Each compiled problem retains its own read-only chain_matrix and immutable chain_index, and provides problem.to_building_levels(z) for mapping chain coordinates. Later changes to the source DataFrame do not affect the optimizer or compiled constraints. No recipes are normalized. Shared configurations receive the sum of contributions. problem.evaluate(z) returns an ordinary building-based EconomyState, and problem.objective(z) returns the negative selected equilibrium metric.

Scenario constraints are transformed into chain coordinates: A @ C @ z <= b and A_eq @ C @ z == b_eq. Building bounds remain enforced; any chain using a prohibited configuration is fixed to zero. Feasibility, boundedness, and the nominal GDP warm-start LP are evaluated in this restricted chain space. Production matrices, workforce, wealth seeds, and returned state arrays retain the economy's original indexes. Final verification checks the selected chain vector, its physical building levels, and the original building constraints.

GDP, GDP per capita, average wealth, equilibrium tolerances, COBYLA options, hard budgets, and failure diagnostics follow EquilibriumOptimizer. x0 and result.x use chain coordinates; result.building_levels and state.building_levels use building coordinates. The raw solver_result retains COBYLA's internal reduced/scaled coordinates. Budget exhaustion can return the best verified equilibrium with result.success=False.

Fixed recipes restrict the feasible production space. They coordinate upstream and downstream changes but do not guarantee balanced household demand or profitable individual buildings. Financial flags remain diagnostics. See the era-5 chain example for a matrix loaded from the comparison example's building_levels.csv and reproducible output artifacts.

docs.title: Parsing game data
docs.text: For column meanings, units, and defaults, see the parser dictionary and the complete production-table dictionary.

docs.title: Generate the tables
docs.text:
Run the comprehensive examples/parse.py script from the project root to generate all parsed game tables and the buy-package charts:

uv run python -m examples.parse

You can also run it directly with uv run examples/parse.py. Outputs write to artifacts/datasets/parsed/. The buy-package CSV is stored at artifacts/datasets/parsed/buy_packages/buy_packages.csv, with its linear and log-scale charts in the adjacent figures/ directory. These charts are views of the parsed dataset.

Initialize the pinned artifact submodule before running the examples:

git submodule update --init --recursive

Regenerate in dependency order: run examples/parse.py first, then examples/production_analysis.py, then the desired analysis scripts. Existing files at old artifact paths are not used as fallback inputs.

Generated data follows your installed game version

Regenerating a CSV may change many rows when the installed Victoria 3 version differs from the committed snapshot. Review those changes before replacing tracked data.

docs.title: Use individual parsers
docs.text:
Call individual parsers when you need tables in memory for a Python analysis. The package searches common Steam library locations on Windows, Linux, and macOS. If detection fails, pass game_dir="/path/to/Victoria 3/game" to the parser constructor or function.

For example, BuildingsParser exposes to_dataframe(), while goods() returns a DataFrame directly:

from vic3_analysis import BuildingsParser, goods

buildings_df = BuildingsParser().to_dataframe()
goods_df = goods()

print(buildings_df.head())
print(goods_df.head())

For other parsers and their parameters, see the parsing API reference.

docs.title: Build the production table
docs.text:
The production table remains a separate step using the generated CSVs:

uv run examples/production_analysis.py

production_table() iterates through every possible building and production method combination, then analyzes the resulting goods flows, employment, and other metrics. For further explanation of the columns, see the production-table dictionary.

The above script reads artifacts/datasets/parsed/ and writes artifacts/datasets/production/production_table.csv. You can also build the production table directly from the parsers:

from vic3_analysis import (
    BuildingsParser,
    PopTypesParser,
    ProductionMethodParser,
    goods,
    production_table,
    technology,
)

df_production = production_table(
    BuildingsParser().to_dataframe(),
    goods(),
    ProductionMethodParser().to_dataframe(),
    technology(),
    PopTypesParser().to_dataframe(),
)
df_production.to_csv("production_table.csv", index=False)

The technology and pop-types tables are optional enrichments. Without the technology table, production_table() keeps the raw unlocking_tech keys but omits era and unlocking_tech_localization. Without the pop-types table, it omits wage_normalized_employment and profit_per_wage_normalized_employment_nominal. For example, a base table needs only the first three inputs:

df_production = production_table(buildings_df, goods_df, production_methods_df)

To add wage-normalized metrics without technology enrichment, pass pop types by keyword:

df_production = production_table(
    buildings_df,
    goods_df,
    production_methods_df,
    df_pop_types=pop_types_df,
)

docs.title: Add localization
docs.text:
Localization is opt-in. Pass Victoria 3's internal language name to a parser to add a nullable localization column beside each identifier, while retaining the original script keys for joins and analysis:

from vic3_analysis import BuildingsParser, goods

goods_df = goods(language="english")
buildings_df = BuildingsParser().to_dataframe(language="english")

The localized values are the raw strings from the game files: references, formatting, icons, and localization functions are preserved. Missing entries are pd.NA; no fallback language is applied. Use localization("english") for the complete catalog, including related keys such as technology/building descriptions and lens-option suffixes.

production_table() propagates localization columns when its input tables contain them. Economy(language="english") applies the same option only to tables it parses internally; explicitly supplied DataFrames remain unchanged. Localization does not change the default no-language behavior.

See the parsing API for constructor parameters, return values, and exceptions.

docs.title: Supply-chain analysis
docs.text:
The supply-chain data dictionary defines every report column, its scope, units, formulas, and failure behavior.

SupplyChainAnalyzer runs one nominal optimization for one terminal good and returns an immutable result. The scenario must have positive exports of terminal_good and an enabled min_goods_balance. Other exports are allowed as background demand; imports may cover some or all terminal exports. Graphs focus on the terminal chain, while system metrics include all solved configurations.

from vic3_analysis import Economy, Scenario, SupplyChainAnalyzer

economy = Economy()
scenario = Scenario(
    name="automobiles",
    min_goods_balance=0.0,
    goods_export=(("automobiles", 1.0),),
    objective="automation",
)
result = SupplyChainAnalyzer(economy, scenario, "automobiles").run()

The result snapshots the compiled matrices, solved state, production metadata, and HiGHS diagnostics. Later changes to the economy or another optimizer do not change it.

docs.title: Inspect tables and graphs
docs.text:
headline = result.summary()
goods = result.goods()
processes = result.processes()
flows = result.flows()
workforce = result.workforce()
constraints = result.constraints()
bottlenecks = result.bottlenecks()
alternatives = result.alternatives("automobiles")
graph = result.graph()

Every table has a stable schema, including when it is empty. Process economics retain exact coproduct contributions. The API does not silently allocate a multi-output process's value to individual goods.

The summary treats the chain as one production unit: it reports GDP per worker, GDP per wage-equivalent worker, and GDP per construction point in weekly and annual units. Wage-normalized employment sums the production table's private-wage coefficients over solved levels; missing contributing coefficients make wage metrics unavailable (NaN). These ratios use aggregate totals rather than averaging individual buildings' ratios. Matching system_ fields cover all solved activity, including processes outside the terminal chain.

Extraction buildings have separate chain_levels_<building> and chain_levels_per_10k_pop_<building> fields, plus their system_ equivalents. For example, chain_levels_per_10k_pop_building_coal_mine reports coal-mine levels per 10,000 chain workers. Multiple PM configurations of one building type are combined; fractional levels remain fractional. Resource columns cover all extraction types in the economy in sorted identifier order, including banned or unused types with zero levels. Empty and failed sweeps retain these columns; failures use NaN. Population means employed workers, and known zero denominators yield zero. Agricultural land remains a separate metric.

Two graph views are available:

  • realized is the default and contains active configurations upstream of the terminal good.
  • allowed contains technology choices not disabled by era, PM bans, building-group bans, or zero building limits. It is not a claim that every route is independently LP-feasible.

Both are cyclic bipartite NetworkX graphs: goods point to consuming production configurations, and configurations point to output goods. Cycles remain strongly connected components; they are never relabeled as raw-resource leaves. graph() returns a defensive copy.

docs.title: Why the graph uses processes
docs.text:
Normally we would say an Economy contains a set of buildings. However, since a building key can appear in several times with different production methods, we choose to rename it to processes.

This terminology follows the process/product distinction explained in Brightway's inventory documentation. Brightway is a Python life cycle assessment (LCA) framework whose inventory model separates transformations from the products they consume and supply. Here, production configurations are the transformations and Victoria 3 goods are the products. Brightway also uses activity in its API; its glossary shows that this term has broader usage than just production processes.

Consequently, process:<configuration-key> identifies a node, building remains its source metadata, and result.processes() reports configuration economics. The term does not mean an operating-system process.

The supply-chain design references compare this architecture with Brightway, PyPSA, Calliope, pymrio, and openLCA. They explain the shared ideas behind graphs, optimization, economic accounting, and explicit coproduct treatment, together with the limits of each comparison.

docs.title: Sweep all producible goods
docs.text:
from vic3_analysis import Scenario, sweep_supply_chains

template = Scenario(
    name="era_3",
    min_goods_balance=0.0,
    objective="construction_cost",
    era_cap=3,
)
sweep = sweep_supply_chains(
    economy,
    template,
    target_value=100_000.0,
    keep_results=True,
)

summary = sweep.summary
failures = sweep.failures
automobiles = sweep.result_for("automobiles")

For each good, the sweep uses the higher of its aggregated template exports and target_value / base_price. It retains all other exports and all imports. For a generated quantity of 100, template exports of 20 become 100, while exports of 150 remain 150. target_quantity and target_base_value report the effective terminal exports, including on failure rows.

By default, the sweep follows economy.producible_goods order. Infeasible or unbounded goods become failure rows and do not abort later runs. Execution is sequential.

Open the supply-chain showcase for committed outputs and regeneration commands. The supply-chain API documents every public type.

docs.title: 名词解释
docs.text:
• 需求大类，即 BV1pG3yzVE67 中的“消费组”。
  • 消费额，即每张图的纵轴，为每10,000名劳动人口在该需求大类上的每周基础价格预算，并非实际市场支出或商品数量。受扶养人口的基础消费权重为劳动人口的一半。
  • 财富等级，即每张图的横轴，决定了一个人每周的消费总预算是多少。当收入无法负担当前消费组时，财富等级会下降；能够负担更高等级的消费组时，财富等级会上升。与生活水平（SoL）强相关但不相等。

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
• Need categories are the “consumption groups” discussed in BV1pG3yzVE67.
  • Consumption, the vertical axis of each chart, is the weekly base-price budget for that need category per 10,000 working adults, rather than actual market spending or goods quantities. Dependents have half the baseline consumption weight of working adults.
  • Wealth level, the horizontal axis of each chart, determines a person's total weekly consumption budget. Wealth falls when income cannot cover the current buy package and rises when income can cover a higher-level package. It is closely related to standard of living (SoL), but the two are not identical.

See the parsing guide for setup and game-file detection, and the buy-package data dictionary for field definitions. The data and findings are verified for 1.13.11 and 1.15; regenerated outputs depend on the installed game version.

docs.title: Million-worker equilibrium wealth search
docs.text: examples/optimize_equilibrium.py uses EquilibriumOptimizer to search for the highest average wealth found while household wealth, consumption, prices, and finances settle together. The search is deterministic and local; its result does not establish a global maximum.

docs.title: Scenario and inputs
docs.text:
The worker cap is 1,000,000, and the workforce ratio is 0.4, allowing up to 2,500,000 people including dependents. Actual employment may be lower. The scenario excludes DEFAULT_BANNED_BGS from examples/__init__.py, and uses min_goods_balance=None. Infrastructure is unconstrained (min_net_infrastructure=None); usage remains visible in reports as a diagnostic, and the summary records an empty minimum.

Fixed throughput multipliers are all 1.0, and level-dependent economy-of-scale bonuses are disabled. Trade, resource limits, arable-land limits, and era restrictions retain their defaults. Household demand is endogenous, calculated from household wealth and population composition.

The script loads the production table, goods, professions, population needs, and buy packages from the existing artifact datasets. It restricts production to the union of active building/production-method configurations in the saved era_5_automation/*/processes.csv supply-chain reports. Other configurations are excluded from both the initial mix and the optimizer's search. Generate the datasets and supply-chain reports first:

uv run python -m examples.parse
uv run python -m examples.production_analysis
uv run python -m examples.supply_chain_compare

The initial mix starts with equal levels of every allowed configuration and scales to one million workers without balancing infrastructure. A mix with infrastructure consumption and no supplier is permitted. Missing reports, an empty active set, or configurations absent from the production table raise an error. The optimizer checks scenario feasibility before starting its search.

docs.title: Run the search
docs.text:
The default hard trial budget is 20,000 per local search:

uv run python -m examples.optimize_equilibrium --max-iterations 10

Proportional income tax funds operating losses by default. Disable it with:

uv run python -m examples.optimize_equilibrium --no-subsidize-operating-losses --max-iterations 10

The enabled policy taxes cooperative and dependent income without guaranteeing payroll, and applies to saved baselines and every restart. --resume uses the current invocation's policy, which defaults to enabled; summary.csv records it in subsidize_operating_losses. Imported calls also default to enabled; use run(..., subsidize_operating_losses=False) to disable it. If the initial or saved mix cannot fund its losses, the example still starts the optimizer. Rejected trials receive a penalty based on their funding shortfall; only verified, funded equilibria can become the best solution. An unfunded saved mix is not retained as a baseline. The summary records initial_equilibrium_status=insufficient_income and leaves its initial wealth/GDP metrics empty. If no valid result is found within the trial budget, the search fails without overwriting exports. Other initialization errors still propagate. See tax-funded operating losses.

Direct-file execution is also supported. A short run can validate the pipeline and regenerate reviewable snapshots:

uv run python examples/optimize_equilibrium.py --max-evaluations 8 --max-iterations 1

The CLI enables timestamped INFO progress on stderr by default, with periodic summaries every 100 trials. Use a shorter interval for a small-budget run:

uv run python -m examples.optimize_equilibrium --max-evaluations 8 --max-iterations 1 --log-every 2

--log-level DEBUG adds individual trial outcomes, new incumbents, and concise inner-solver start/finish/failure messages. --log-level WARNING suppresses the progress logs while retaining the printed result summary. --log-every must be positive. Imported calls to run(..., log_every=100) leave logging configuration to their caller. Standard logging stream handlers flush each record, so progress appears as the search runs; redirect stderr to save it.

Progress reports distinguish initialization from subsequent search, show uncached trials used versus budget, current and best unscaled objective values in weekly units, scenario feasibility, inner-solver iteration counts, failures, and elapsed seconds. See the progress-field reference. The CSV schemas and annualization rules are unaffected by logging options.

After each completed search, the example reduces materially loss-making building configurations by --loss-reduction (default 0.5) and restarts with a fresh trial budget. Profitability uses all output revenue, including coproducts, minus input costs at the returned equilibrium prices, with the same absolute/relative loss tolerance as the supply-chain example. Other levels are unchanged, and employment is not scaled back up. The adjusted mix must remain feasible under the scenario's worker cap and building exclusions.

Iteration stops when the returned objective is strictly lower than the preceding search's objective. The scenario maximizes average wealth; GDP remains a reported metric. Equal objectives continue, and the earliest result wins ties. --max-iterations optionally caps completed local searches. Omission means unlimited searches, so an equal-objective plateau can continue indefinitely. --loss-reduction 0 disables reductions for all restarts.

To start from the saved solution:

uv run python -m examples.optimize_equilibrium --resume --loss-reduction 0.5 --max-iterations 10

Resume aligns buildings.csv by building and production method, restores omitted zero configurations, and validates the saved levels against the current scenario. Duplicate or unknown configurations are rejected. The saved levels are re-evaluated, then adjusted for the first local search. The saved baseline remains eligible as the best solution; if the first new result is worse, iteration stops and exports that baseline. Use --resume --loss-reduction 0 --max-iterations 1 for one local search from the unchanged saved levels.

The budget limits optimizer trials. Evaluation of the initial baseline and fresh verification of the returned state are additional equilibrium solves. A very small budget can end during search initialization and retain the initial mix. Larger budgets can take tens of minutes or longer.

The console reports each search's initial and returned objective, the best objective, annual GDP, actual workers and population, and iteration termination. A budget-limited search retains its best verified equilibrium with search_success=False and an explicit search_message; equilibrium_status is still converged. Invalid inputs or a search without a feasible converged state raise an error before writing new outputs. Financial flags remain visible on successful household equilibria.

docs.title: Summary and solution
docs.text:
The summary has one row per completed local search, including the worse attempt that triggers stopping. A resumed invocation also has an iteration-zero row for the re-evaluated saved baseline with empty search diagnostics. Each row records scenario settings, starting and returned metrics, search diagnostics, financial-flag counts, applied reduction, objective change, UTC start time, and elapsed seconds. is_best selects the row whose solution is exported. Every row also records invocation totals, the selected best iteration, optional iteration cap, and stop reason (objective_worsened or max_iterations). Monetary totals use equilibrium market prices; annual GDP is weekly GDP multiplied by 52. See the summary dictionary for all columns.
